guides.title: Adding an accent colour
guides.summary: A small patch of one contrasting colour gives the eye a resting point and makes a plain model look finished.
body: Steel, leather and browns on their own make a flat model. Pick one colour that is not yet on it, ideally from the far side of the colour wheel from the main colour. A brown flask on an all-blue figure, or a red sash on a grey one, is enough.

Use it in small amounts only: a gem, a lens, a stripe, a few dots on cloth or a touch of verdigris on bronze. Give these few spots more care and saturation than the big areas, since they carry the whole model.
Put the strongest use of it on the upper half, near the face or head. That is what people see first on the table, and accents on the legs are easy to miss.

Echo it two or three more times in duller or smaller forms, roughly in a triangle around the model, so it does not look stranded. A lone bright spot at the very edge, such as on a foot, pulls the eye away and traps it there.

If one accent grabs too much attention, either repeat it somewhere else, for example as a shadow tone in skin, or push it toward a colour already on the model. Matching effects, such as glowing eyes and glowing runes, should share one colour.
For a gem or lens: base in the accent, shade the lower half with your darkest colour, then add a small light dot in the top corner.
On a grimy, muted model, let the accent stay clean: after weathering, touch the pure colour back onto its raised parts.
Next to red or orange, choose a warm egg-yolk yellow rather than a cool lemon. Once the accent is in, resist adding more contrasting colours.

guides.title: Yellowed, dirty white
guides.summary: Age finished white with sepia or brown washes, stippled dirt and streaks for a grimy look.
body: Finish the white as usual with its grey shading first. The grey gives depth.
For aged, yellowed white, apply a sepia or light brown wash over the top. It tints the white towards a worn yellow.
For a cooler, lightly grimy white, use a blue-grey wash thinned half and half with water over the whole area, then pick the raised edges back out in white where the wash dulled them.
For grimy shields and panels, shade a pale warm grey with a grey-brown, mixed into a softer glaze towards the bottom and around rivets.
Stipple thin glazes of the shade colours along the bottom edge for a muddy texture.
Highlight edges and rivets with white and add small chips at the same time. A dot of dark brown inside a few chips makes them read as older, deeper damage.
Pull fine downward streaks of light brown from rivets for subtle staining. Use this for anything meant to look old or neglected.

guides.title: Why you rarely need pure white
guides.summary: Near-whites and very light greys read as white, look less stark, and leave room for a brighter last touch.
body: Almost nothing real is pure white. Light, shadow and reflections tint it, so near-whites read as white on a model. White paint is also coarse and tends to go on chalky and patchy.

Save pure white for the very last small highlight on edges and top surfaces, roughly the top tenth, and for tiny glints such as an eye catchlight or the hotspot on a gem. That small amount makes the eye read the whole area as white.
For everything else use near-whites: off-white greys, creams, or pale tints of blue, green or pink. Next to darker, stronger colours they still read as white and add a little colour interest.

For a white panel, base in a very light grey. Next to black it looks fully white and leaves pure white free for the highlight. Shade it with a brown wash run only into the recess, not over the whole panel.

Mixing white into a colour to highlight it greys it and kills its strength, and skin soon looks chalky and dead. Lift skin and warm colours with a pale yellow, ivory or a pale skin tone, and keep the brightest layers very small.
Choose the near-white to suit the light: ivory, bone or sand for warm sunlight, a pale blue or cool grey for snow and ice.
Pure white corner dots on dark colours can look stark. A very light grey with a touch of white blends better and still catches the eye.
Switching temperature makes highlights look brighter: a slightly warm yellowish white for the broad midtone, then a pale cool grey for the highlight, or the reverse.

guides.title: Base colours for heavy weathering
guides.summary: Start base colours paler and greyer than the finish you want, so oils, grime and texture do not swamp the model.
body: Washes, filters, oils and grime all darken and mute what is underneath. A colour that looks right before weathering often ends up dull and dark after it.

Choose base colours a step lighter and a little greyer than the finish you want. Small models already look darker than the real thing, so this helps twice. If your colours come in graded shades, base with the lighter one. You can add strength back later with a glaze.
Start with strong light. Prime black, then put a heavy white zenithal on from above with an airbrush or a large dry brush. Dirt and texture only read over a bright start.
For coloured armour, a dark ink of the colour sprayed from below and a very pale tint of it from above fades more richly than priming in the colour itself.
Keep a big value gap between light and dark areas placed close together, so the model still reads at table distance once it is dirty.
Keep small details darker than the armour and avoid loud colours on them. Save the few strong spots, such as lenses, until the weathering is done.
Mixing one shared colour, such as a pale pinkish flesh, into the highlights of several areas helps a heavily weathered model hold together.
Match the grime to the colour. Black hides dirt but shows crisp grey edges and small metal chips; yellow and orange need brown grime settled in the recesses and strong dark lines to stay readable.

guides.title: Base colours that suit the model
guides.summary: Choose ground colours that complement the model, glaze the model's colours onto the base, and keep base details quiet.
body: Keep the model's main colour off the base, or the figure loses its outline: a grey armoured figure on grey rubble disappears. Pick a different colour family, such as sand or earth under grey, or cold blue ground under a red figure.
A plain grey base can make the model look separate from it. Thin the model's main colours to glazes and touch them in random patches on stones. Keep it subtle; it fades as it dries.

Echo the model's colours on the base, a little less strong than on the model: a green tuft, a thin orange pigment, a purple-grey rim. A colour opposite the model's main one works well, such as orange dust in the recesses under blue armour.
Match the model's overall level of colour. A vivid model on a dull grey base looks wrong, so allow the base a bit more colour than feels natural.

Keep the base slightly darker, duller and less busy than the model so the figure stays the focus, but still give it dark recesses and bright raised edges so it has shape. Small models need stronger contrast to read. If a base looks too loud, knock it back with a wash or a duller dry brush.
Paint every part of the base from one related palette, and give tufts and moss a light dry brush so they match. Vary repeated details such as leaves with two or three slightly different browns.
Dull bright debris such as dropped helmets or weapons with heavy brown washes, then add only the odd bright edge.
A black or dark coloured rim gives a clean frame. Once you settle on a base scheme, keep it the same across a whole group of models.

guides.title: Choosing colours that blend well
guides.summary: Colours close in hue, or similar in strength, blend smoothly; opposites go muddy unless glazed.
body: Two colours of the same hue but different strength blend without trouble, as does a colour blended towards black.
Different hues can still blend if they are similarly muted, such as a dusty pink into a dusty green. Before blending two hues, adjust one until both are close in brightness.
A muted yellow into a strong magenta fights. Bring them closer first, for example by adding white to the magenta.
Wet blending physically mixes the paints, so opposite colours make a muddy middle (red into blue gives a purple band). Glaze the transition instead.
Paints made from a single pigment mix cleaner than paints made from several. If a mix keeps going grey or brown, the pigments are fighting; use simpler colours where the blend must stay clean.
To move between two hues by brush, let the first colour run a little past the join, then push barely thinned layers of the second over it, covering less each time.
For a blend ramp, go from a deep, see-through dark, through mid-coverage middle colours, to pale opaque ones. Paint stripes over black lines on paper to check coverage.
The same plan works in any colour: end purple on a lavender, warm skin on a peach.

guides.title: Breaking up an all-metal model
guides.summary: Use two metals, dark joints, painted plates and one bright accent so a metal model does not read as one mass.
body: A model that is all one metal looks like a shapeless lump. Pick some parts to be other materials, and let one metal be the bright, focal one while the others are toned down.
Use a mid steel for the main parts and a darker metal for others, shading both strongly with a black and brown mix. A touch of matt medium keeps recesses from going shiny.

A few paints give many metal tones: black or brown into silver for darker steel, brown into gold for a rich warm base, a little gold and silver together for a pale gold. Silver is the stronger, so add it a little at a time.

Vary the undertone and finish as well as the brightness. Some silvers lean cool and blue-grey, others warm and brown; cool reads as clean steel, warm as old or oily iron. A smooth coat on a blade and a dry brush of silver over black on a gun also read as two materials.

For two tones from one silver, wash it all dark brown, repaint the parts you want cleaner, then wash everything black. The twice-washed inner parts go dark and grimy; the repainted parts stay brighter.

On a mostly gold model, pick out raised trim and emblems in a paler, whiter gold, or pair copper trim with bronze panels. Paint flexible joints, hoses, seals and tyres black, and some plates as flat colour such as off-white.
Add one or two small spots of strong colour, like a red valve, lights or a painted symbol. Give that colour contrast as strong as the metal's, so the metal does not take over.
Base coat all the new areas first to judge the balance before highlighting anything. Paint symbols after the metal, then tidy around them with the metal.

guides.title: Brightening dark historical colours
guides.summary: Accurate dark uniforms blur together on small models, so push them brighter and add small bright details.
body: Dark green with black kit and brown wood can merge into a shapeless mass at arm's length.

Paint the main colour a little brighter and lighter than the real reference so it reads, since small models look darker than they are. This also leaves room for washes to pull it back down. Over a black primer, give it at least two thin coats so it covers evenly.
Pick out small bright details such as coloured cords, cuffs or white piping to separate the dark areas.
Highlight black straps with a few short dark grey lines.
Exact accuracy matters less than it seems. Real paint varied between batches, crews and seasons, and sun and dust shifted it further, so a colour that looks right to you is fine.
Small variations in mixed colours across a unit look natural and do not need to match exactly. Keep the overall colour consistent across the whole force.

guides.title: Checking values with a greyscale photo
guides.summary: Take a photo in black and white to see if areas are too light, too dark or blend into each other.
body: Strong colours make brightness hard to judge by eye. Two very different colours can share the same lightness and merge at arm's length, and most of what painters call contrast is value: how light or dark each area is.
Light the model evenly, photograph it, and turn the saturation to zero with the phone's mono filter or any editor. If it reads well in greyscale, it will nearly always work in colour.

Each main area, such as skin, cloth and metal, should separate clearly from its neighbours. If two look the same grey, lighten the highlight on one or darken the area beside it. Edge highlights and dark lining are the usual tools.
For a quick check without a camera, hold the model at arm's length and squint, then turn it on its side, upside down and round the back. Weak areas often show from angles you never paint from.
For a harder test, shrink or blur the photo to mimic table distance. Fine edge lines and small freehand disappear, so the big light and dark pattern has to work on its own.

The brightest point and the strongest contrast should be where you want the eye, such as the face, fading away from it. On a glow effect, make the glow about as bright as the brightest skin highlight and keep the shadows near it darker.

Common fixes: skin often needs deeper shadow, metal painted with flat colour needs brighter highlights, and reds need pushing darker or lighter. A value change usually does more for a muddy model than more detail.
Fix the biggest problem first, glazing lighter or darker over it, then photograph and check again.

guides.title: Choosing colours for chips
guides.summary: Dark chips on light surfaces, light or warm chips on black, and a mix of both on mid colours.
body: Light colours such as white, cream or yellow: chip with a single dark brown or charcoal. Dab it with the side of the brush in an uneven pattern along edges.
Mid to bright colours: combine light chips for scuffs with dark chips for deeper damage. Add a fine light line along the lower edge of each dark chip where the new edge catches the light.
Black and very dark colours: a darker chip barely shows. Use the highlight grey, a warm brown that suggests primer, or metallic paint for bare metal.
On dark colours, two-tone chipping gets busy. Keep to one step, or tiny nicks of the highlight colour.
Metal in the deepest scratches suggests bare metal. On light armour, ring it with a darker brown first.

Play temperature against the armour. On blue and other cool colours, a warm reddish brown (#6b3a2a) shows from a distance and reads as rust; a near-black brown suits red but looks heavy under a mid blue. On a warm colour, a slightly cooler chip stands out more. Test on a spare part if unsure.
Paint chips on black in the same grey while you highlight, and add a little rust brown around rivets.

guides.title: Choosing a colour scheme
guides.summary: For a single model, decide the setting, mood and key part first, then alternate warm and cool areas around it.
body: Start with the setting or a one-line story: where the figure is and what it is doing. A snowy base or a dusty road shapes the rest. With no story, write two or three mood words, such as grim, calm or savage, and pick colours that carry them.

If you still have no plan, paint one focal part first, such as the face or a mask, and let it guide the rest. Know roughly what you like before asking others for ideas, or the advice will pull you in every direction.

Give one main colour most of the coloured areas, roughly 70 percent, and a contrasting second colour about 30 percent, or try 60, 30 and 10 with a small accent. An even split tends to look stiff. Leather and wood can count as dull versions of a warm main colour.

A reliable pairing is the colour opposite on the wheel at a similar strength: blue with orange, red with green, purple with yellow. A punchy blue wants a punchy orange, not a pale peach. Alternate warm and cool areas around the model.

Check the set has a light, a dark, a bright and a dull colour. Too little contrast looks muddy, too much looks garish, and no dark at all looks washed out. If one colour must stay, such as a vivid red skin, keep it off the next biggest area.

Put a little of the opposite temperature into each area, such as warm browns in the shading of cool armour. Keep straps, rocks and small bits neutral, and avoid a third vivid colour. One tiny contrasting spot, like green eyes on red, adds focus.

Make sure the eye goes to the head: light tones near it, distracting detail around it toned down. Colours lifted from a picture, poster or flag work well if you copy roughly how much of it each colour covers.
Once all the base coats are on, look at the whole model before washing. That is the easiest moment to change a colour. If you always reach for the same colours, pick a new main colour on purpose.

guides.title: Choosing a wash colour
guides.summary: Pick a wash that matches what the base colour turns into in shadow, and give different materials their own wash.
body: Ask what the base colour looks like when it darkens. A mid red darkened drifts towards a deep brown, so a brown wash suits it better than black, which can make it look dirty and grey.

As a starting rule: warm brown for reds, oranges, yellows, wood and skin; black or a dark blue-grey for steel and cool greys; a deep version of the colour itself for blues, greens and purples. A purple or crimson wash adds depth to gold, and a green wash suits green skin.

On vehicles and armour panels, a dark brown wash usually looks more natural than black, which can look harsh, and it hints at dust and grime too. Go deeper on dark greens and lighter on sand and yellow.
One wash over one base coat gives three tones: the plain base on raised parts, a lightly tinted base on flat areas, and deep shadow where it gathers.
One wash over the whole model is quick but makes every colour look alike and a little dirty. For a cleaner finish, give each colour group its own wash.
Work group by group: wash the main colour first, then base the silver and black details and wash only those black, then base the gold and give it a warm chestnut wash.

To tell textured materials apart, highlight wood, leather and cloth with the same couple of colours, then tint each with a different wash, such as warm brown on wood and a greenish or purple wash on the others.

Thinned ordinary paint can stand in for a ready-made wash. It should stain the surface, not cover it. A skin wash straight from the pot is often too strong on pale skin, so thin it with medium and build it in coats. Mix brown and black for a dirtier, worn look.

guides.title: Choosing colours for an army
guides.summary: Pick a main, a secondary and a spot colour for the whole force, then prove the scheme on one test model.
body: Start from an idea rather than the box art: a film, an insect, a bird, a comic, a flag, or simply a colour you love. A strong idea is often one simple contrast, such as glossy black shell against pale flesh.
Choose a main colour for the big surfaces, a secondary colour for cloth or trim, and one spot colour that appears on every model. Paint everything else in neutrals such as grey, brown and metal.

Keep the core simple enough to repeat across dozens of models, with room for extra detail on leaders and big pieces. Strong pairings such as yellow and black read well on the table; too many colours look busy at arm's length.

Try the colour opposite your main colour on the colour wheel as the spot colour. Put blobs of the candidates side by side on the palette, or colour a grey photo of a model roughly in an image editor, to judge the balance before you commit.

Paint one test model start to finish, ideally the most complicated one in the range so every material gets decided. Write down every step, and drop or change any step that is slow or does not work. If it fails, strip it and try again.
Big monsters and vehicles can bring brightness to a dark force, but reuse the same few paints, lighten every colour with the same pale tone, and swap any extra colour for one already on the models.
Then paint the rest from your written list without stopping to deliberate.

guides.title: Choosing a highlight colour
guides.summary: Lighten a colour with a lighter neighbouring hue, a pastel, cream or bone instead of white so highlights stay vivid.
body: Mixing white into a colour lightens it but also greys it. Red plus white turns pink, and pale blue can make a turquoise chalky. Lighten with a lighter hue instead.

Pick the lightener from a neighbour on the colour wheel, not the opposite. Yellow or a warm orange keeps red rich. A pale blue keeps purple vivid, while a yellowish off-white dulls it. Pale yellow into turquoise gives a bright, fresh highlight.

For warm colours try pale yellow, pale sand, ivory or a light skin tone; for cool colours a sky blue or mint. About a third pink or light skin tone keeps a red highlight warm. Black takes a warm pinkish highlight or a cold blue one, which lets two black areas look different.

Using one light colour, such as a pale sand, to highlight several areas ties the figure together; add a little more of it for each step. To make one item stand apart, give it a different light colour on purpose. A dark shell highlighted with a strong blue reads apart from pale cloth highlighted with white.
Test before you commit. Mix the midtone with two or three candidates side by side. A warm off-white gives a quiet, natural finish; a stronger hue gives a punchier one.
For calm or dark areas, such as burgundy cloth or back scales, lighten with a light grey so the highlight stays muted next to brighter parts. Keep the palest step to tips and points.
For the last tiny highlight, mix a little pale bone or cream into the highlight colour, thin it, and flick it onto corners and sharp points only. Keep pure white for a few specks.
Pale highlights can look chalky at first. Push them anyway, then pull the colour back with thin glazes of the mid colour or an ink, which also smooths the steps.

guides.title: Cold light and night scenes
guides.summary: Highlight with a mid-value turquoise or blue instead of white or pale yellow so a model looks lit by moonlight.
body: A highlight only has to be lighter than what surrounds it. It does not have to be white or pale yellow.

Moonlight needs three things: one light direction, a cold pale blue light, and low saturation in every colour. Prime with a zenithal from the moon's direction and paint the face first, then use it as the guide for where light falls elsewhere.
Keep the usual base colours, but highlight every material with the same cold colour, such as a turquoise or a pale pastel blue (#b8cde0), so it reads as one light.
Push the shadows and midtones darker first. Lowering the whole range makes a mid-value turquoise read as bright.
Keep the shadows warm against the cold light: deep black with violet or purple worked in, and a touch of red in places. Pale skin takes cold highlights with warm shadows well.
Leave a little colour so the model stays interesting, and glaze some of the midtone back over at the end to pull everything together.
The same trick with orange or yellow ochre highlights suggests torchlight or sunset.

guides.title: Tying colours together by mixing
guides.summary: Mix a mother colour, or colours already on the model, into the others so every part belongs together.
body: Areas in totally unrelated colours make a model look disjointed. Shared tints fix this without being obvious.

Mother colour: pick one colour that sets the mood and add a little of it to every mix, including skin, metal and base. Base coating the whole model in it first is the simplest start. A mix that looks loud on the palette looks calm on the model once everything shares it.

Borrow colours for shading. The dark green of the armour in the shade of red cloth gives a rich shadow and links the two. A single dark blue-black mixed into any colour also works, darkening and greying it at once like real shadow. Yellow needs far less of it than other colours.
Mix a touch of one area's colour into another's midtone, such as the warm brown from the gold into a green cloak. It links the two and calms a colour that is too bright.

Use one pale colour, such as ivory, a pale tan or a pastel yellow, as the top highlight for most materials: mix it about half and half into each base, then more for the last step. Test it on the main colour first, since some mixes look sickly, and add strong pale paints in tiny amounts.

Start every area from one shared dark and finish towards one shared light. The middle colours can then differ a lot and still belong. Over a one-coat paint, add a little of it to the first highlight so the two match.

Choose neutrals from what is already on the palette: a warm brown is close to red plus black, and greys can be mixed from black and a scheme colour. Keep the number of browns and greys low or the model turns muddy. Reuse kept mixes on leather, cloth or the base.

To add a new colour without clashing, mix one of the main colours into it, such as the leather brown into a turquoise cloth. The same mother colour across a group makes the models look like they come from the same place.

guides.title: Painting the colour of the light
guides.summary: Warm, cold or coloured light tints every colour it falls on, so decide the light before you pick highlights.
body: There is no single true colour for an object. A white wall in a photo holds almost no pure white, skin looks pale under office light and tanned at sunset, and a red car changes between sun and cloud.
Decide where the light comes from and how warm or cool it is before you highlight, then place highlights and shadows to match.
Soft ambient light, such as daylight or room light, keeps each material's own colour and only tints the highlights. Warm light gives warm highlights, and its shadows lean cool.
A strong coloured source, such as a blue glow, recolours everything in its reach. Skin, metal, bone and cloth all turn towards blue where it falls.
One of each on a model, such as a cool glow from below and warm light from above, looks striking. Keep a band of dark shadow where the two meet; that gap makes both lights believable.
To see where light falls, put a desk lamp over the model from the direction you want and take a photo. It is a ready-made map for your highlights and shadows.

Water and distance act like a coloured light. For an underwater scene or a far-off part of a diorama, push the colours toward blue and lose the reds and oranges first, keeping the nearest parts the most vivid.

guides.title: Building a scheme from reference art
guides.summary: Pull a small palette from artwork, photos or one loud colour you like, and paint the whole model from it.
body: Pick an illustration, film still or photo whose colours you like. It does not need to match the model's theme: a ship, a sunset, an animal, a historical uniform or a fashion photo all give ready-made palettes, often less obvious than other painted models. Keep a folder of pieces that grab you.
Use a colour picker on a digital copy to pull out about five main colours. Nudge them towards the pure tones rather than the in-between mixes.

Find the closest paints you have; near enough is fine. To match by eye, zoom in and hold paint pots against the picture. Check the reference first: web photos are often colour-shifted, so find a second, better photo before matching.

Put all five on the palette, plus black and white if needed, from the start. Try them as swatches side by side before they go on the model. Look at the whole artwork, including background and side figures, for how the colours are used.

When the shapes differ, copy the rules rather than the layout. Note the dominant colour, where the accents sit (top, underside, edges) and how they follow the body, then apply that to the model's own plates and limbs. If sources disagree, take the overall feel.

Keep the reference large and in view the whole time, and hold the model beside it now and then. Differences in richness are obvious side by side. If an area looks dull next to it, glaze a strong colour over it.
Small models need more contrast than a picture. Highlights and reflections that look right in the art often need to go lighter on the model.

Another route: start from one loud colour you rarely use, such as a hot pink, and build around it with one colour that suits it, set against black and white. Either way, give the focal area, often the face, the strongest contrast.

guides.title: Colour variation in skin
guides.summary: Tint set zones of the face and body with thin reds, blues and purples so skin is not one flat tone.
body: One brown wash gives skin a single dull shadow colour. Real skin is translucent and shows warm and cool zones, so add them with very thin glazes, mixed partly from the skin tone itself so no change is abrupt. Shading with dark blue or green mixed into the skin tone, rather than black or brown, already helps.
The face has rough bands: a slightly yellow forehead, a red band across the nose, cheeks and ears, and a cooler, duller chin. Go lightly on the nose or the figure looks drunk.

Mix a deep red with some skin tone into a thin glaze. Put it around the nose, mouth and bottom lip, into the corners of the eyes and the shadow under the cheekbones, not on the cheeks themselves. Pinker tones also suit ears and the skin around scars.

Glaze a thin blue-grey, soft purple or cool blue-green just under or above the eyes, like a hint of eye shadow. A cool grey-blue or green on the sides and lower third of the face suggests stubble; on a smooth face a faint purple works better.

On the body, keep yellow where bone sits close under the skin, red on elbows, knees, knuckles and palms, and blue or purple in deep shadow such as armpits and the waistline. A very thin magenta filter in the lower half of big muscles stops shadows going brown or grey.

On a finished blend, thin filters can do the whole job: warm yellow over all but the brightest highlights, then a reddish brown and a purple-red into smaller shadow areas each time, and a dark blue only in the deepest shadow away from the light.

The face will look heavily made up at this point. That is expected. Glaze the highlight colours thinly back over the raised areas so the colour looks under the skin, not on top. Judge it again once the colours around it are painted.

On big areas of skin, mix in a little of its opposite (red into green skin gives a muted purple) for lips, elbows and knuckles. Darker skin takes the same zones more subtly, older skin shows more blue, and sickly green or purple glazes suggest bruising.

guides.title: Rich variety within one colour
guides.summary: Layer several hues under a final colour so a single-colour area feels rich rather than flat.
body: Real materials are never one flat colour. Light, reflections and texture all add variety.
Paint a range of colours underneath: greens, pinks, oranges, purples, placed loosely where they suit the form.
Then glaze the intended colour over the top in thin coats. The area still reads as that colour, but with depth.
Keep the glaze thin so the colours beneath are not lost.
This suits monster skin, hide and large single-colour areas, where flat colour shows most.

guides.title: Colour wheel harmonies
guides.summary: Use complementary, triad and split-complementary sets, or a gamut mask, to decide which colours go in a scheme.
body: On the painter's wheel, red, yellow and blue mix into orange, green and violet, with in-between tertiaries such as blue-green. Black, white and grey change value, not hue. Pigments differ in strength, so equal parts is only a starting point.

Complementary: two colours opposite each other, which make each other look more vivid. Analogous: a narrow wedge of neighbours, calm and low in contrast. Monochrome: one hue in light, mid and dark versions; it suits one model, but add texture or pattern to keep it interesting.

Triad: three evenly spaced, such as green, orange and purple. Split-complementary: one colour plus the two either side of its opposite, strong contrast with less tension. Tetradic and square schemes use four colours and easily look busy.

Turn a triad or split-complementary guide around the wheel, printed or in an online tool, until you find a set you like, or borrow one from a sunset. Mix the chosen colours on the palette to see the whole range before you touch the model, and judge the result by eye.
Whatever the harmony, let one colour dominate and use the others as small pops. Scatter each pop colour in two to four places, such as bracers, a knee and a tassel, for balance.

Slightly muted versions sit together better than full-strength ones, so add a touch of a neutral if they fight. Corners do not need to be strong colours; a dull blue-green works as well as a bright yellow.
A gamut mask is a shape laid over the wheel, such as a triangle. Its corners are your colours, and anything mixable from them plus black and white is allowed.

Colours need not be literal: bronze counts as a dull yellow-orange, and browns, blacks, whites, belts and boots are neutrals outside the scheme. If a type of model always ends up one colour, try the one opposite it on the wheel for a fresh look.

guides.title: Controlling saturation
guides.summary: Mixing dulls colour, and a pale grey final highlight tames a colour that has become too strong.
body: Saturation is how strong a colour is, how far from grey. Brightness is how light or dark it is. Pink is a lighter red, not a stronger one. A colour is usually strongest in its midtones, and a lot of white or black dulls it.
Mixing two bright colours gives a result duller than either. The more colours in a mix, the closer it moves to grey.
To dull a colour on purpose, add a neutral grey, a touch of black, a pale highlight colour, or a little of its opposite. Too much of the opposite shifts the hue.

Use muted mixes for most areas and keep your most intense colour unmixed for the one spot you want to pop. A strong colour next to a greyed one is contrast in its own right, and among muted ones it looks almost as if it glows. If a model feels flat despite good highlights, grey down the large, less important areas.

Colour lives in the midtones, so very dark shadows and very bright highlights leave an area reading duller. Light layered straight over very dark goes grey for the same reason; to keep a colour clean, start from a midtone and work up and down from it.
Bright colours that suit small gaming figures can look garish on busts and large models. A drop of grey makes them look natural.

If highlights built from a coloured mix have made an area too strongly tinted, for example black that now looks bright blue, finish with a pale, cool grey on the top edges only. It pulls the area back towards neutral while keeping it crisp.

guides.title: Essential first colours
guides.summary: About fifteen colours, including black, white, primaries, earths, two metals and two washes, cover a first army.
body: Start with black and white. A strong white, #f4f4f0, is the most used pot on the desk. A soft black, #1e1e1e, covers shadows, mixes and lining.
Add three primaries that mix cleanly: a warm red, #b3261e, a mid blue, #1f4f9a, and a golden yellow, #e8b923. Between them you get oranges, greens and purples.
Then the earth colours that cover wood, leather, hair, fur and bases: a mid brown, #6b4a2b, a dark brown, #3a2617, and a pale bone, #d8c9a3.
A mid green, #3f6b35, and a mid grey, #7a7d80, save a lot of mixing on armour, cloth, stone and plants. A warm skin tone, #c98d6b, with a wash covers most faces.
Add one silver, #a8acb0, and one gold, #b08d3c, for metal, plus a brown wash, #4a3320, and a black wash, #202020, for shading.
Then add the main colour of your own scheme, and a darker and lighter step of it if you would rather not mix them.
Mix the rest. Greys from black and white, pinks from red and white, olives from green and brown. A short set teaches you more about colour than a wall of pots.

guides.title: Fantasy heroes: knight, wizard, ranger, elf, dwarf
guides.summary: Each classic fantasy hero type has a colour approach that fits it; pick one main colour, support it, and save one accent.
body: Knight: let the steel lead. Use a mid steel grey, #8a8f94, shaded dark, and one bold colour on the shield, tabard or plume, such as a deep red, #8b1e1e, or a royal blue, #24438f. Two colours plus steel looks noble. Four looks like a jester.

Wizard: the robe carries the model. Pick one rich colour, such as a deep purple, #4b2a6b, or a midnight blue, #1c2a4a, with a pale cream trim, #e8dcb5. Save the brightest colour for the staff gem or spell, and tint the nearby hands and face with it.

Ranger: earthy and muted. Use greens and browns that differ in lightness, such as a moss green, #4f5d32, a leather brown, #6b4a2f, and a dusty grey brown, #7a6f5e. Dirty the cloak hem. One small cool accent, such as grey blue fletching, #6f8290, stops it reading as mud.

Elf: clean, pale and elegant. Use cool pale skin, #e9d6c8, light cloth such as an ivory, #efe9d8, or a sea green, #3f8f7f, and fine gold or silver trim. Keep blends smooth and edges crisp, and go light on grime. The slim sculpt suits small careful detail.

Dwarf: warm and heavy. Ruddy skin, #c98a6b, a big beard in a rusty red, #a8452a, a dark brown, #4a2f1e, or a grey white, #c9c6bf, and warm metals such as bronze, #8c6239. Shade the beard deeply and highlight the braids so it does not become one flat blob.
The face sells the hero. Give the nose, brow and cheekbones a slightly brighter highlight than the rest of the model, and keep your accent colour close to the head.
For a party of heroes, give each one a different main colour but repeat one shared colour, such as the same leather brown, so they look like they belong together.
Let the props tell the role. Swords, staffs, bows and axes already say who the figure is, so the paint only has to support them, not shout over them.

guides.title: Blue, red and other fantasy skin
guides.summary: Any colour can work as skin if a warm flesh note sits in the top highlight or the deepest shadows.
body: Blue, red, purple or grey skin reads as living flesh mainly because of the final highlight. Mix a warm tan or flesh colour into it, or use it neat on the tips of the nose, cheeks, brow, lips and knuckles. Pick out the raised parts where light would land and leave the rest.

On cold skins such as blue, mix the flesh tone with a cool grey so the highlight feels organic but still icy. Red skin looks best with slightly dulled shadows and a warm ivory highlight. White markings stand out well on a strong blue.

Keep a warm undertone in the deepest shadows. Underpainting with a warm berry red and building the cool colour up over it, leaving the red in the recesses, works well. A deep pink base under orange skin does the same job.

Add a flush where skin is thin: cheeks, lips, nose, knuckles and elbows. Use a soft red or pink on warm skins and a purple or very thin magenta on cold ones; over blue, magenta reads as a rich purple. Glaze the mid colour lightly back over to blend.
For very dark skin, such as a purple-black, slip a different hue like pink into the midtones and highlight to a very pale cold blue, then glaze back with a red-violet until smooth.

A quick route is a one-coat paint over a pale base. Purple over bone, then layered mixes of purple and pale flesh, gives lilac skin. Blue over clean pale skin, highlighted up to a pale verdigris green, gives an eerie glow. Charcoal or stone-grey skin is a black one-coat paint over a lighter grey.

If a strong unnatural colour looks garish, highlight it towards a cooler neighbour instead of a brighter version of itself, such as a little sky blue into yellow-green. Use the same light colour on hair and horns.

For skin in several colours, plan the zones from reference first. Where two zones meet, keep the true colour in the recesses and the lighter one on raised parts. A cool skin set against warm, weathered gear stands out strongly. Green skin has its own entry.

guides.title: Creating a focal point
guides.summary: Draw the eye to the face or key area with the brightest colour and sharpest highlights, and keep the rest quieter.
body: Decide the one or two areas people should look at first, from what the model is about. A rider on a beast is about the rider's head and the beast's face. More than two points compete.

Put the most saturated colours and brightest, sharpest highlights there, and let colours darken and calm down away from it. Keep the lightest values high on the model, around the head and chest, with the lower body darker, so the eye drifts up.

Bend reality where it helps. Make the face lighter than the rest of the skin, nudge a reflection towards the head, and keep arms, legs or a backpack darker than the light would really leave them. Believable beats strictly correct.

Temperature works too: on a mostly warm model make the face or key detail cool, or put one warm spot on a cool model. A pink tongue on a grey face, or small bright jewellery near the face, leads the eye up.

Tame anything that competes. Start a big flag or cloak that should be bright red from a muted base, and avoid a glowing puddle on the base. High contrast everywhere just looks busy, so save it for the parts that deserve it.

Keep minor details quieter: one or two clear highlights and at most one shadow each, and less vivid than the focus. Keep bone and skulls muted, with restrained whites, so they add contrast without stealing the eye.

Some painters do the focal area first so it sets the brightest point for the rest; others leave the most eye-catching details until last to judge how strong they need to be. Either way, check the balance at the end.

In a group or diorama, put more highlights on parts near the main figure and fewer further away. Short on time? Give the face or weapon your best work and the rest a solid standard. A small glow on lenses or a blade, or one neat freehand border, makes a plain model look finished.

guides.title: Shifting a colour with a glaze
guides.summary: A thin glaze over a finished area can warm, deepen, saturate or fix its colour while keeping the shading underneath.
body: Use transparent paint for this: an ink, a one-coat paint, a wash or a regular paint thinned well with glaze medium. Thinned washes are the most forgiving to start with. Even a bright opaque paint adds a pale cast.

To fix a colour: yellow over painted gold that looks like wood, a warm tan over boots that came out too cool, a bright red over a dull red, yellow over a light green that looks too cold, and a transparent blue over flat black that looks grey. A colour that drifted rarely needs stripping.

A filter over part of an area shifts its hue rather than darkening it. A thin green over the lower half of armour and a different tint over the top give a convincing fade. Glazes also set mood: orange or red pulls a scheme warmer, blue or purple cools it, and warm brown over silver ages it.

To restore saturation lost to whitened highlights, give the area one all-over glaze of a rich colour, or push a heavily thinned vivid paint of the same hue into the shadows only. Do this before edge highlighting.

For variety, glaze a heavily thinned warm brown or yellow in a few patches, especially low on cloth, or touch a faint contrasting colour into the midtones only, such as pink into a cool blue. On pale areas such as bone, keep warm filters out of the highlights. A colour borrowed from elsewhere on the model ties it together.

To recolour finished cloth, brush a transparent one-coat paint over pale, highlighted areas. Red over cream may look pink at first; a second coat and a wash deepen it, and the shading underneath carries through.

Load the brush, dab most of it off, and stroke from the highlight towards the shadow so pigment builds where the stroke ends. Do not go back into a wet glaze; let it dry and add another pass. One-coat paints pool under a brush, so thin them well.

Glazes and inks knock back the final highlights, so push them a little brighter first and re-apply the brightest edges and dots afterwards. For a display finish, alternate highlighting and glazing a few times; for quick models, glaze once.

guides.title: Highlighting black
guides.summary: Highlight black with greys or tinted colours in small, sharp steps, and leave enough black showing to still read as black.
body: Black reads as black only when most of the surface stays dark. The share of dark to light matters more than the exact grey, so make each highlight stage smaller and tighter than the last.

Start with a very dark grey on the main folds and edges as a chunky first stage; it sets where the light falls. Then a mid grey as a finer line on the highest parts, and a light grey only on the sharpest edges. Edges facing the light get brighter lines than those in shadow.

Keep each stage thin and add in-between mixes if a step looks too big. If black reads as blue or grey, the highlights cover too much: trim them back with thinned black and leave more black between. Changing the tint rarely fixes it. If it looks flat instead, add a mid step or a lighter top edge.

Pick the tint for the material and its neighbours: cool blue-greys for hard shiny armour and beside red; black with a touch of pink, cream or pale yellow for leather, gloves and robes, which reads as light rather than dust; neutral greys for anything. A teal or very dark green ties black into a scheme. Two black items with different tints stay apart.

Finish with a few small dots of light grey with a touch of white on corners. On smooth panels, slip a second colour such as blue or purple between the highlight and the black so reflections do not look plain grey.

Fast options: one cool mid grey for every black part, varying only how much area you cover; three greys placed in shrinking areas without blending; or a dark grey stippled onto raised areas, then lighter greys dry brushed on edges. A one-coat black over pale primer gives soft highlights for free.
For worn black, dab short broken grey marks along edges instead of a clean line. A few small silver chips show up best of all on black, and can stand in for edge highlights when time is short.

For subtle colour, glaze very thin purple or red over the panels in places, then restore the sharpest highlights. On a dull, dark model or one with lots of grey, stop before pale grey so the black parts keep their weight.

guides.title: Highlighting gold, bronze and copper
guides.summary: Highlight warm metals with a pale gold rather than silver so they keep their colour.
body: Silver highlights on gold, bronze or copper are shiny, but the colour looks out of place. A pale, slightly muted gold suits yellow gold, bronze and copper alike.
Base in a warm mid gold and shade it with a warm brown or red-brown wash, which suits gold better than black. Then layer the gold back over the flats, keeping out of the recesses next to rims.

Edge the sharpest points with the pale gold first, using the side of the brush on raised edges and the tip on tight ones. Then thin it further, blot the brush almost dry and glaze it over the flats you want brighter.
Choose a highlight metallic with fine flakes that thins well and stays smooth, not grainy.

If you want the extra shine of silver, step towards it in mixes, half gold and half silver, then mostly silver on smaller areas, and keep pure silver to the last tiny edges and dots. If it looks flashy, a thinned brown wash or a glaze of the gold blends it back.

On painted copper and bronze, white turns a red-brown salmon pink. Build the lights with orange and then a warm yellow, use white only for the last small reflections, and glaze the orange back if the pink spreads.
To make a polished part stand out, give the flat of a blade a paler gold than the rest, or break up a large gold shield with a second, darker metal on its patterns.
Even a little matt black on a mostly metal model makes the metal look brighter. On steel, a bright fine silver is right for highlights, small scratches and dots.

guides.title: Changing hue from shadow to highlight
guides.summary: Use a different hue for shadows and highlights, not just darker and lighter, for richer colour.
body: Shadows and highlights do not have to be darker and lighter versions of the base colour. A different hue works as long as the value is right; check it in a greyscale photo.

A simple ramp starts from a deep, cool version of the colour and ends on a warm, pale one, with about three steps between, such as a dark greenish blue to a pale yellow. Set the colours in a row on the palette so halfway mixes are easy. Avoid steps that contain black, which go dull.
Or pair a naturally dark colour with a naturally bright one, such as a dark purple and a yellow-green. Base coat in the dark colour and highlight by mixing in more of the bright one.
Glaze see-through paints over this undercoat to set the final colour. The hue shift shows through.

Some pairings that work: brown shaded with a pinky purple and highlighted to a warm yellow; green skin with pink and red in the shadows; grey metal with a hint of turquoise; peach skin shaded to red-brown, with a muted purple only in the darkest areas.
Lighten greens with a yellowish bone or yellow rather than white, which turns them chalky. Most yellows are fairly transparent, so they cover less but blend more easily.
Shade neutrals with a little of the dark colour and highlight them with a little of the bright one, so everything shares the shift.
Shading towards blue or purple and highlighting towards yellow gives contrast in both lightness and hue. Keep it subtle; the viewer should not spot the trick.

guides.title: Hue, value and saturation explained
guides.summary: Every colour has a hue, a value (how light or dark) and a saturation (how intense), and each can change on its own.
body: Hue is the colour family itself, its place on the colour wheel: red, blue, yellow and so on. Navy and sky blue share the same hue.
Value is how light or dark a colour is. A pale pink is high in value, a deep wine red low. Value does most of the work of light and shadow on a model, and a black and white photo shows it on its own.

Saturation is how intense or pure a colour is. A neon green is highly saturated, a grey hardly at all. Paint straight from the pot is usually at its most saturated; mixing in other colours tends to dull it.

The three move separately. Adding white raises value but lowers saturation, which is why red plus white turns pink rather than a brighter red. A touch of the opposite colour, a grey or an earthy brown calms a colour that is too loud.

Contrast is how different two colours are, and it can come from any of the three: black against white is strong value contrast, violet against yellow strong hue contrast, a vivid colour beside a greyed one saturation contrast. Red against orange has very little.
Use them to steer the eye. Put the strongest value contrast and the most saturated colour on the focal point, and keep hues and values quieter elsewhere.

guides.title: Judging colours next to their neighbours
guides.summary: Block in nearby colours early, because a colour looks different against bare primer than on the finished model.
body: A colour seen against grey or white primer looks different from how it will look on the finished model. A pale skin next to pale primer is especially hard to judge.

Before finishing an area, rough in the main colours that touch it, such as the hair, cloth and armour around a face. Do deep recesses and parts that sit under others first, then block each main area in until no primer shows, like painting by numbers.
Then decide whether the area needs more warmth, more contrast or less saturation. Settle the overall tone first, then refine faces, scars and edges.
Lay these early colours fairly thick so you see the result in one coat. If a colour is wrong, you find out before building up four thin layers.

Early on, the aim is the right colours in the right places, not perfect blends or zero mistakes. Expect it to look rough. Squint to check it reads right, for example whether metal already looks shiny, then start refining. Once everything is blocked in, adjusting a colour is quick.

guides.title: Keeping colours bright and saturated
guides.summary: Start with saturated colours, shade each colour with a wash of its own family, and avoid heavy dark washes.
body: Pick saturated starting colours, a little brighter than the result you want, over a pale undercoat. A coat over a darker one comes out duller, and over a lighter one brighter. A muted yellow will never become a vivid one; it is far easier to tone a bright model down than to add colour to a dull one.

Shade each colour with its own family: red wash on red, a warm yellow tint on yellow, chestnut brown on gold. Keep black washes for metal, black and white. Many dark paints contain black and muddy a colour, so a richer, deeper version of the same hue makes a better shadow.
Mix strong washes about half and half with medium so they flow but darken less. A shadow paint thinned about four parts water to one of paint can be run into folds and downward faces.

Avoid over-washing. A heavy all-over wash at the end darkens everything evenly and is the usual reason a model looks murky. On bright armour, wash only the black, the silver and a few deep vents, stopping right at the edge of the bright colour.

Layer each base colour back over the raised areas, leaving wash only in the shadows, then highlight upwards. Push final highlights hard: the brightest yellow or pink you have, or green with white for an almost neon edge.

If a colour has gone dull, mix a wash from a coloured shade, a one-coat paint of the same colour and medium, roughly one to one to two, with a drop of ink if it is still weak. Two thin coats beat one heavy one.

For a focal feature, build colour with several coats of a thinned bright paint, each covering a smaller area, so it is strongest at the tips. Small colourful touches, such as a cool purple glaze low on a warm surface, add interest without dulling.

guides.title: Leaving room for highlights
guides.summary: Choose a base or mid tone dark enough that a brighter highlight is still left to reach.
body: If your base is pure white, there is nothing brighter to highlight with. Start from a cool off-white instead: a pale grey primer with a thinned blue-grey one-coat paint over it, tidied with an off-white, leaves pure white for the sharpest edges. A pure white base only suits areas a wash alone will finish.
If your brightest orange or yellow is the base, highlights drift towards bone. Start from a deeper version.
It is the jump up to a much brighter tone on edges and peaks that makes a colour read, not the base colour itself. You use very little of that brightest colour.

The opposite mistake also happens. On a very dark colour, a base that is too dark leaves the edge highlights nothing to work against and the model reads as black; too light and it turns into a brighter, different hue. Try the base and both highlights on a spare piece first.
On the most important areas, such as the face or helmet, add a little white to the last highlight for extra punch.
Shade bright colours with a brown wash heavily thinned with medium. Strong wash stains them too much.
Prime white or bone under pale and bright colours. Orange and yellow cover poorly over dark.

guides.title: Painting with a limited palette
guides.summary: Put out a handful of paints plus black and white and mix everything from them for harmony and speed.
body: Pick around five or six paints before you start and do not add more. Black and white are always allowed. One hue family covers more than it seems: brown is a dark orange, and pink is a light red.

Choose a clear run from light to dark, mostly warm or mostly cool, plus one contrasting accent. A handy five is one warm, one cool, two neutrals and one accent. Keep any one model to two or three prominent colours with neutrals for the rest; a tiny touch of gold barely counts.
Use your darkest paint as the shadow and your lightest as the highlight for every area. A very dark brown and a pale flesh read as black and white when set against each other.

A classic four-colour set is a strong red, black, ivory and yellow ochre. Ochre with some red and ivory makes flesh, and a touch of black cools its shadows. Ivory cut with ochre and a little black gives a dirty off-white. Highlight red with ochre and ivory, not white, or it turns pink.

Mix freely and try uneven ratios. Two contrasting colours mixed often give a useful grey, such as green into dark brown for metal. For belts and boots, mix a neutral from a colour already out plus black and a touch of yellow or orange rather than hunting for a brown.

When mixing a transition between two colours, add a little of the base colour to both so the steps are gentler. Paints with one or two pigments stay cleaner when mixed. Save your brightest, purest colour for one job, such as the eyes.

Because every colour shares the same mixes, skin, cloth and props sit together naturally. On a group, use the main and accent colour straight from the pot so they match, and mix the small details freely. Close enough reads as the same.

Swatch the set side by side on palette paper before you start, since colours change with their neighbours. If the set feels too narrow halfway through, widen it a little rather than giving up on the idea.

guides.title: Lips, blush and makeup
guides.summary: Small touches of colour on lips, eyelids and under the cheekbones add life to a face.
body: Paint the skin fully first, then add colour on top.

Paint thin red on both lips following their shape. Highlight the bottom lip with red mixed with a pale yellow to make pink, then add a tiny pale reflection point. Do not wipe out the top lip with too bright a highlight; shape the dip in its centre.

On small or male faces, colour on both lips can look swollen. Tint only the lower lip, mix the lip colour with skin tone so it stays close to the skin, or use a muted purple mixed from red and dark blue. A slightly thinned bright red one-coat paint over the skin also gives a natural tint.

For eye colour, use a cool shade that contrasts with warm lips, such as a turquoise or blue mixed with some skin tone. Glaze it thinly on the lids, blending up towards the brow. A thin purple glaze also reads as eyeshadow.

For eyeliner, block the eye in dark grey rather than black and leave a ring of it round the white. For a smoky look, put thinned black around the eye above and on the lower lid, with a fine bright skin line along the lashes.

Glaze a soft pink mixed from pink and skin tone under the cheekbones or on the upper cheeks towards the front of the face. Test it over a patch of skin colour on the palette first. If it looks painted on, glaze a thin skin tone back over it. A pale chalky tone gives a powdered, period look.

For heavy face paint, lay it thin enough over the finished skin that the shading still reads. Work dark eye makeup from the inside out, using black with a little blue, leave a gap of skin below the eye, and let colour creep into wrinkles as sweat would carry it.
Less is more. Use as much or as little as suits the figure. Makeup guides are a good reference for where light and shadow go.

guides.title: Making leaders and ranks stand out
guides.summary: Set leaders and specialists apart with more accent colour, one marked detail, upgrade parts or a fancier base.
body: Pick one small detail every model has, such as a plume, sash or feather tip. Leave it plain on the rank and file and tint it in the accent colour on leaders.

Use the amount of an accent colour to show rank. With two accents, such as gold and turquoise, give troops more turquoise and only small gold touches, and give leaders more gold, extra edge highlights on it and stripes in the other colour.

Without a uniform, colour still shows who matters: drab browns and greys for the lowest ranks, one bright garment for better equipped fighters, and trims and simple freehand patterns only on the elite.

For group markings, pick one fixed spot, such as a knee pad or helmet, and a simple rule, like a stripe or a different helmet colour for leaders. Keep markings within the existing colours, and choose a freehand shape you can repeat if no transfer exists.

Specialists can share the scheme but shift it. A thinned sepia wash turns white armour to ivory; thinned black over white, then a mid grey dry brush, gives charcoal for stealthy models. Trim painted over the darker base comes out muted.
Reversing the scheme on a leader, swapping which areas are light and which are dark, marks it out at once. Swapped heads, weapons or upgrade parts from the spares box add to it.
Save detailed bases for leaders and centrepieces, and give the rest a simpler version in the same colours so everything still matches.

guides.title: Using colour to separate materials
guides.summary: Pick colours and finishes so leather, cloth, metal and armour read as different materials.
body: Neighbouring areas in similar colours blur into one mass at arm's length. Give touching areas clearly different colours or values, and if a model is mostly two materials, such as skin and shell, make one light and one dark. Step back to check each part still reads.

Where several areas are already black, more black detail merges into one mass, so paint belts and straps as brown leather. The reverse also holds: next to bright cloth, near-black belts make the colour look brighter than mid-brown leather would.
Tint neutrals to suit the main colour: a neutral brown next to yellow rather than an orange one, browns leaning orange against blue, greys leaning green next to red.

On a model built from one colour family, vary it: a bright red for cloth and a deeper red for armour, warm or cold browns for jacket, straps, hair and wood, or slightly different greys for a grey uniform's cloth, armour and webbing. Highlight each with its own lighter shade.

When cloth and a hard surface share a colour, start the cloth darker, give it a warmer highlight and soft blends, and give the hard surface a paler, cooler highlight with crisp edges, taken towards ivory on the tops of curved plates. Two whites can be split the same way.

Finish changes how a colour reads. Tiny, very bright highlights make black look like shiny leather, and fine lines across fur suggest texture. Matt varnish on cloth beside slightly glossier armour, with a dark line where the two meet, separates them further.
Add scratches or texture so leather looks different from armour. Small steel chips on black armour plates, with the leather left plain black, set them apart at a glance.

Check small details against what sits behind them: parchment on cream robes should go almost white, and skin next to gold and blond hair reads better pushed towards pink. For speed, one recipe for both is fine; the difference is a finishing touch.

guides.title: What goes under metallic paint
guides.summary: Smooth surfaces and the right base colour make metallics shinier and truer, such as black under silver and brown under copper.
body: Metallics need a smooth surface to shine. A very matt primer scatters light; a satin primer under metal areas helps. Metal also shows every mould line and scratch, so clean up carefully before priming.

How much the undercoat colour matters depends on how thickly the metal goes on. Under two solid coats it barely shows, so any primer that suits the rest of the model is fine, and a well-flowing metallic covers white primer easily. Under a thin, see-through coat it tints the metal.

For thin coats, silver looks most like silver over black. A blue-black leans it cold, a brown-black leans it towards old iron. A glossy black under a thin metal coat looks noticeably shinier than a flat black.
Gold, bronze and copper look richer and cover in fewer coats over a brown, such as a mid brown (#6b5a3a) or a reddish brown for copper. Yellow under most metals looks poor.

Mixing a little of the base colour into the first metallic coat helps it cover. Expect the first coat to look dull; the shine appears once the dark is hidden. Golds and pale bronzes often need three or more thin coats. That is normal. Do not over-thin to speed it up: the flakes spread unevenly and look blotchy.
Block non-metal areas and recesses in thinned black and paint or dry brush metal only on raised parts. The recesses stay shaded with no wash, and you never have to work metal into every crack.
Over white, a very thin metallic settles into recesses and the white edges act as highlights, but those bright edges are not real shine. Go over them with a thin metallic.
On a model that is mostly metal, a metallic spray primer can prime and base coat in one step.

guides.title: Mixing your own shades and highlights
guides.summary: Mix lighter and darker steps of a colour from paints you own, by parts, instead of hunting for exact paints.
body: You rarely need a separate paint for every step. Start from the paint nearest your base, darken it with a little of a deeper related colour or a brown, and lighten it with a pale colour you already use. If you have no darker version, base mixed half and half with black works as a shade. Black overpowers fast, so add it in tiny amounts.

For highlights, a pale bone, cream or ivory keeps steps warm and natural, where white goes cold and chalky faster. Red turns pink with any pale mix, so lighten it sparingly with a skin tone or orange. A lighter paint of the same family, mixed half and half with the base, gives the cleanest step.

Some useful mixes: bone into yellow for a pale yellow; bone half and half with black for a mid grey to edge black cloth; a little brown into bright red for a dull shadow; a dark brown with light orange added bit by bit for a warm brown; red with a touch of green for an earthy pink for lips and tongues.

A part is any equal blob of paint; the back of a brush handle moves small, even amounts. For a ladder, mix three to one, two to one, one to one and so on in separate pools. With dropper bottles, count drops and write the ratio down so you can mix it again. If two steps look too far apart, mix a little of each together.

To match a colour you do not own, take the closest paint and add tiny amounts of a second colour, testing swatches against the reference. Close is good enough. A one-coat paint can tint a mix, but a large share of it makes the mix behave oddly.
A paint that covers well but is not quite the right colour is worth keeping. Tweak it by mixing rather than looking for another.
Keep mixes on a wet palette so they last across a whole group; small differences between models do not show. When wetting paint from the sponge, watch for stray colour creeping in.
Do not stall hunting for the exact paint someone else used. A similar colour on a painted model beats a perfect one waiting on the shelf, and technique matters far more.
