guides.title: Mixing tinted blacks
guides.summary: Black mixed with a little colour, or mixed from dark colours, looks richer and ties a part to the rest of the model.
body: Put several small blobs of black on the palette and mix a different colour into each, such as a purple, a dark green or a turquoise.
Strong colours need only a little. Hold each mix next to the model and keep the one that suits it.
A dark blue mixed with a dark brown makes a richer black than black paint alone.
Paint it thinly and judge again after any wash. Too close to the main colour can look flat.
Highlight gently, for example with a little ivory. Matt gear needs only a small highlight.
A smooth grey mixed from a warm off-white and a cool black reads well on weapons and tech.

guides.title: Mixing greys and browns from opposites
guides.summary: Opposite colours cancel into rich greys and browns, which shade and dull colours more gently than black.
body: The three painting primaries are red, yellow and blue. Mix two and you get a secondary: orange, green or purple. Each secondary sits opposite the primary it leaves out.
Mixing a colour with its opposite cancels it out. Red and green, blue and orange, or yellow and purple give browns and greys, depending on the balance.
For a brown, start with orange and add a little blue. More blue gives a cooler, darker brown; more red or yellow a warmer one. Add white for tans, and black only if you must.
For a grey, mix the opposites close to even and add white. A little more blue gives a cool grey, #6f7782; a little more orange gives a warm grey, #857a6e.
Use a little of the opposite to dull a colour that is too bright. A drop of green in a red shadow, rather than black, keeps it rich instead of dirty.
Mixing all three primaries gives a dark, muddy neutral. A touch of it in every shadow mix helps tie a scheme together.
Real paints are not pure primaries, so results vary. Test on the palette first and note the ratio that worked.

guides.title: Mixing one-coat paints
guides.summary: Mix one-coat paints together for custom colours or softer coverage, or with white for a bright colour that covers.
body: One-coat contrast-style paints mix with each other like normal paint. Blend a couple of yellows and reds for a custom orange rather than hunting for one exact pot.

They behave very differently: some act like a soft wash, some like a strong ink, some cover heavily. Ones with a pale deposit settled at the bottom of the pot usually cover more. Choose the one that flows best and is close in colour, then tint it with a little of another.

Mix a transparent one with a strong one to set the coverage. The weak one lets more of the undercoat or metal show through; the strong one gives richer colour but hides more. Add medium for more transparency, or less to cover faster.

Mix in a thick white for a bright colour that covers black in about three thin layers. A little white also makes a very runny paint easier to place for highlights. Leave white out of anything meant to work as a glaze.
Some mixes cover weakly. If a colour looks thin, a second coat or a single stronger pot may work better.
Test every new mix in a hidden spot, such as under an arm or on the feet, and wipe it off while still wet if it is wrong. Mix enough for the whole batch so every model matches.

guides.title: Mixing and choosing skin tones
guides.summary: Mix any skin tone from a red, a yellow, a blue and an off-white, and nudge it warmer, pinker, sickly or cold.
body: Nearly all living skin sits in the warm orange to brown range. Build it from a fairly pure red, yellow and blue plus an off-white. You do not need paints sold for skin; any browns, oranges and blues you own will do, guided by a reference photo.
Mix a little red into a lot of yellow for a bright orange. Red is much stronger, so add it sparingly. Orange plus off-white gives a standard light, warm skin.

Red plus blue gives a deep brown, the base for very dark skin. Lift it with off-white for a cool, purplish dark brown, or mix in some of the orange for a warmer one. For olive and mid tones, combine that brown with the orange and white mix and a little extra yellow.

A quicker start is a mid brown lifted with white to the tone you want, plus a very small touch of red-brown so it does not look grey. Ready-made flesh paints are often weak, too yellow or too orange, and very bright flesh looks fake, so mute it a little with grey. Mix plenty, as you will keep coming back to it.

A touch more red gives pinker skin. A touch of blue cools it; let the yellow dominate and it turns sickly. If a flesh paint looks orange, mix in a light cool blue: up to about four parts in ten for pale, delicate skin, a fifth for weathered skin. Once the highlights start to look blue, switch to white.

Pink and green cancel towards a believable neutral, so a warm flesh mixed with a dark green makes a deep green-brown shadow, and with a light green a natural mid-tone. Shift the ratio to control how warm the skin looks.

Match the light rather than using one mix for every face. Warm sun: ochre and orange midtones, brown shadows, yellowish highlights. Cold: pink midtones, blue or violet shadows, greyish highlights. Purple and brown mixed equally make a clean cool shadow. Darker skin often shows bigger jumps between light and dark.

Mix the base first, then glaze pure colours on top for subtle shifts; a thin warm brown glaze over the finished face ties the tones together. Keep a photo of a real face nearby to see where skin is pinker or more yellow.

guides.title: Muted colours that make accents pop
guides.summary: Keep most of a model muted or desaturated so a few vivid areas stand out and busy schemes calm down.
body: Lots of strong colours side by side compete, and the model looks chaotic. If everything stands out, nothing does, so decide which part should lead. Muted does not mean dark: a quiet or gritty scheme still needs punch, from deep recesses against sharp pale edges.

Give that part the vivid, pure colours. Paint gear, bags, wood and the rest of the cloth in dull natural tones: grey, olive, blue-grey, dull brown or black. Small details can take muted versions of the scheme colours, such as a greyish green under a vivid jade, so they stay part of the scheme.

Neutrals are the background: greys, browns, black, white, and any colour greyed down far enough. Brown is a dull orange and skin is orange of varying strength, so both sit easily beside blue. Add a little grey or a mix of the other colours to wood, leather and skin to tone them down to match.

If a pair looks garish, such as red and green, change the brightness, saturation or amount of one. Mostly red with small green lenses reads far better than half and half. A simple route is one main colour, its complement in smaller areas, and everything else grey, black or metal.

Too many metals side by side look noisy. Swap the main one for a flat grey and keep one or two metals for trim and weapons. Bone next to heavy corrosion or other loud effects works better darker and grimier.

Paint areas that should recede, such as shield backs and the inside of a mail skirt, in a dark brown along with the leather. Under a bright rider, keep a big mount muted in a complementary hue, with small touches of the main colour on claws or markings.
Before finishing, check there are enough small pops of pure colour on gems, orbs or weapons. Paint them over white so they reach full brightness.

A clashing many-colour scheme can still work if the technique is neat, the head carries one strong colour and the base stays dark and neutral. A scheme often looks awful at the base coat stage; it usually comes together once shaded and highlighted.

guides.title: Choosing a colour for a glow
guides.summary: Cyan, turquoise, yellow, orange and green glow easily; plain blue needs so much white it loses colour.
body: A glow needs a very light core. Plain blue has to take lots of white to get there and goes pale and chalky.
Cyan and turquoise are naturally lighter, so they need less white and stay saturated.
For yellow, orange or green glows, a pale yellow can serve as the bright core without losing saturation.

Build the ramp from a deeper neighbour on the colour wheel. The outer edge, where the light barely reaches, sits one or two steps towards the cooler, deeper side: a yellow glow starts from orange or red, a yellow-green from a blue-green, a blue-green from a blue-violet.
Work inwards: thinned deep colour, pure deep colour, a mix of deep and main colour, the pure main colour, then a very pale version of it or white at the source.

A glow shows best on a darker surface. Pick a glow colour that contrasts with, or complements, what it lights, and slip in a neighbouring second hue, such as purple beside blue, for a richer effect. Colour also sets the mood: cool blue reads as technology, warm light as fire, purple as magic.
Fluorescent paints can help but are not needed.

guides.title: Paint changes colour as it dries
guides.summary: Acrylics usually dry a little darker and duller than they look wet, so judge a colour only once it is dry.
body: Acrylic paint darkens and dulls slightly as it dries. White and pale colours show this most.
A highlight that looks too bright while wet often ends up just right. Light colours can look a touch less bright again the next day, so check with fresh eyes before adding more.
Thinned paint looks solid while wet and dries far more see-through. Red is the worst for this: it goes on intense and dries showing much of what is underneath.
Let each layer dry fully before you decide to change it or add another coat. A hair dryer on a low setting speeds this up.
Try new paints on a test model or spare piece first so you know how each one dries.
If a colour does end up too bright, a thin glaze of a darker version knocks it back. If deep shadows dried weak, thinned black placed only in the darkest spots fixes them quickly.

guides.title: Painting black areas
guides.summary: Start from a black undercoat, add depth with warm browns low down, and give each black material its own look.
body: Prime black. It does most of the work for black areas, and a heavy dry brush of dark blue grey over it can be enough for a quick black uniform.

Pure black leaves nowhere darker to go, so a flat black area looks dead. Base in a very dark grey, or a very dark blue or teal, such as black and a bright blue mixed one to one, then run thinned pure black into the recesses as the shadow. Lay it in three or four thin coats with little water, or it blotches.

For warmth, drop a heavily thinned dark brown into recesses low on the model. A ready-made brown wash barely shows on black, so mix a little dark brown paint with clear medium; it dries matt like the black. A very deep red works the same way for a richer black.
On cloth, a heavy dry brush of very dark grey, then lighter greys on the edges only. Ragged, broken highlights look like worn cloth and hide a shaky hand.

Give each black material its own treatment. Cloth soaks up light: keep it dark with small, soft, warm grey highlights. Leather has a slight sheen and takes highlights up to a mid grey. Hard armour and metal need the biggest range, with bluish greys up to near white on the sharpest spots only.

Vary how solid the black is. Thinned black over a pale dry brush reads as very dark grey cloth, while a neat second coat on armour reads deep and solid. On a light model, undercoat black details grey first, since a one-coat black is partly see-through and picks up the colour below.
Fine metal chips on black armour tell the eye it is metal, so the black leather beside it stays clearly different.

On a mostly black model, lean soft parts towards a warm brownish black and hard parts towards a cool bluish black, and add one spot colour to break it up. If highlights went too bright, a black wash settles them, but do not wash dry-brushed black fur or cloth.

guides.title: Painting black and charcoal cloth
guides.summary: Base soft dark cloth in an off-black, shade with brown, and build brownish greys gradually on the crease tops.
body: Base in an off-black rather than pure black. It still reads as black but leaves room for darker shading.
A dark brown wash gives a natural, worn look that suits field uniforms. On large areas, layer the off-black back over the flats to remove tide marks.

Build the highlights gradually: start with about two parts black to one part dark grey or brownish grey on the raised folds. Use the side of the brush on hard fold edges and a downward stroke of the tip on soft creases.
Add a little more grey each stage and cover smaller areas, so the transitions stay soft like fabric.

Finish with a sharper mid grey, or a pale blue-grey used sparingly, only on hems, crisp fold tops, knees and shoulders, placed in the centre of the earlier highlight. A cool tone reads as light on black better than a neutral grey.
If the steps look rough, glaze thin black over the cloth and re-touch the top highlights. Keep the greys very matt; a satin sheen makes cloth look like plastic.

Quicker route: over black primer, dry brush a dark grey in several light passes, then tap broken lighter grey highlights onto worn edges. Add a few more after the wash so the older ones show faintly underneath.
An all-black force looks dull. Add an accent colour on ribbons, feathers or straps, or a little brown mud along the hems to break up the black.

guides.title: Painting orange
guides.summary: Keep orange bright by highlighting towards yellow rather than white.
body: Mixing white into orange makes it pastel and dull. Highlight by mixing in yellow instead.
Mix an in-between orange-yellow first so the step is small and the layers go on smoothly.
Finish the highest points in pure yellow.
On hard or metallic-looking parts, add a little white to the yellow right at the end for a shiny, reflective look.
Start from a deeper orange than your brightest one so there is room to highlight, and prime white or pale. Orange covers poorly and loses punch over dark.
For a quick bright orange, mix a one-coat orange with an ordinary orange and lay it in one smooth layer over white primer. The ratio sets how bright and how see-through it is.

guides.title: Painting pink
guides.summary: Pink covers poorly, so paint it over a white or pale undercoat instead of piling on coats or switching paints.
body: Most pink paints are fairly see-through, and fluorescent pinks even more so. Over grey or dark primer they look patchy and dull even after several coats.
Fix the undercoat, not the paint. Lay down white, ivory, or a pale pink or light flesh first, for example as the top layer of a zenithal spray, and the pink goes on clean in one or two thin coats.
Avoid swapping to a chalky pastel pink just for coverage. It covers better but loses the clean, bright look.
Pink is happy over a cool, bluish undercoat gradient, unlike yellow, which needs a warm one underneath.
Shade pink with a deeper pink, magenta or dark red-purple so it stays clean. Brown or black shading makes it look dirty.
Think about what pink says on the model: soft and gentle on skin and cloth, loud and eye-catching on armour or creatures.

guides.title: Painting purple
guides.summary: Shade purple with deep violets instead of black and highlight it with warm pinks so it stays rich.
body: Shade purple with a deeper violet or a dark red-purple rather than black. Black removes colour as well as darkening, so purple shadows turn grey and dull fast.
If you do use black, add only a tiny amount and keep it to the very deepest spot.
Highlight by adding a warm pink or magenta to the purple, or a creamy ivory at about two parts purple to one, rather than pure white. It gives strong contrast without going chalky.
Mixes with a lot of white jump in lightness quickly and push purple towards a cold, chalky lilac. Add the white in small amounts and keep the palest mixes to small, high areas.
For a colder purple, lean the highlights towards a lilac blue instead. Pick one direction and keep it across the whole area.
If highlights drift too pink or too blue, a thin glaze of the base purple over them pulls the colour back together.
For a pale lilac, base in purple and spray or dry brush thin white from above, then glaze thinned purple back into recesses the white flooded, and put a thinned dark violet ink in the deepest folds.

guides.title: Painting red
guides.summary: Shade red with burgundy or dark green rather than black, and finish with a red glaze so highlights stay red.
body: Red covers poorly. Thin it and build two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Over a white or pale undercoat it looks much brighter than over grey or black.

Black alone makes red shadows dull and brownish. Mix a very dark green, blue-green or deep purple into the red for a rich burgundy shadow, and save black for the deepest gaps. A violet wash over deep red also gives cool, rich shadows. Mix a pot of the shadow if you are painting many models.
A brown or black wash makes bright red muddy. Use a deep red wash cut with about one part clear medium to three parts wash, or line the recesses by hand with a slightly runny deep red.

Highlight in small steps, each covering less area. A simple ladder runs from a brown-red mix up to pure red, then a bright orange-red on the top edges. Too much orange or yellow and the red turns orange; too much white and it turns pink. Keep most of the surface red.
For the top highlights, a pale peach, a mid skin tone or a bone colour lightens red without turning it pink. Keep them to the sharpest edges.

Every highlight desaturates red. Finish with one even glaze of a deep red ink or one-coat paint thinned about one to one with medium over the whole area, keeping the brush moving. Pink under a red glaze keeps its lightness but reads as bright red. The same glaze rescues a chalky dry brush.

For the most intense red, paint fluorescent orange or pink over the pale highlights, then glaze thin red over in two or three passes so it glows through. Use it only where you want the brightest colour.

Other routes: stipple white where light hits and glaze red over it in a few passes, or base in a soft orange and shade with red glazes so the orange glows on raised parts. For a cooler crimson, lean towards magenta and set small warm coral details against it.

guides.title: Common hobby and painting terms
guides.summary: Plain meanings of the words beginners keep meeting, from base coat and wash to value, glaze, NMM and WIP.
body: Building colour. Base coat: the first solid, even coat of a colour. Layering: thinned coats on top that build colour, light and shadow in steps. Shading: darker colour in areas that sit in shadow. Highlight: lighter colour on raised parts that catch light. Edge highlight: a thin bright line along sharp edges.

Washes and lining. Wash: thin, see-through paint flooded over an area so it runs into recesses. Pin wash: the same paint placed only in chosen recesses. Contrast-style or one-coat paint: a thin, strong paint that colours and shades in one coat over a light undercoat. Dark lining: a thin dark line where two colours meet, so each part reads as separate.

Blending. Blending: any smooth move between two colours instead of a hard step. Glazing: very thin, see-through paint that tints or smooths what is under it. Feathering: short strokes that fade out at one end. Wet blending: mixing two colours on the model while both are wet. They are often combined, such as a rough wet blend tidied with glazes.

Texture and wear. Dry brushing: wiping most paint off the brush so colour only catches raised texture. Stippling: dabbing small dots with the tip to build texture or a rough blend. Flecking: flicking thinned paint off a stiff brush for tiny spatters. Weathering: chips, rust, streaks, dust or mud that make a model look used.

Light and colour. Value: how light or dark a colour is, ignoring its hue. Contrast: the gap between lights and darks, which helps a model read across a table. Value sketch: blocking in white, greys and black first to map the light. Colour wheel: colours set in a circle to show which sit opposite or side by side.

Metal and glow. TMM, true metallic metal: paint with metal flakes that really shines. NMM, non-metallic metal: faking shiny metal with flat colours and hand-painted reflections. OSL, object source lighting: painting the glow a lamp, fire or spell casts on nearby surfaces. All three depend on careful placing of light and dark.

Prep and tools. Primer: a first coat, sprayed or brushed, that helps paint grip. Zenithal: priming dark, then spraying white or light grey from above, so light and shadow are mapped from the start. Masking: covering part of a model with tape or a removable liquid. Wet palette: a tray with damp paper under a thin sheet that keeps paint wet.

Other shorthand. Viscosity: how thick or runny paint is. Brush control: putting paint exactly where you want it. Freehand: patterns painted straight on. Sketching: loose colour to try ideas. Basing: dressing the ground. WIP: work in progress.

guides.title: Painting white
guides.summary: Build white from tinted greys or shade down from a white base, and keep pure white for the last edges.
body: Pure white is rare in real life. A large area of it has nowhere lighter to go and looks flat, so treat white as a range of light greys and tints. Often only the top half of the surface needs to be truly white.

Building up: start from a mid or light grey, or a pale blue grey, which covers better than white. Lay greyish off-whites over everything but the deepest areas, covering less each time. With an airbrush, spray thinned white in passes over grey, giving panel centres more passes so the grey stays as soft shadow.

Shading down: base in an off-white, then shade with a thin pale blue or grey wash. A black wash straight from the pot turns everything grey, so cut it about half and half with clear medium. Bring white back on the raised areas afterwards.
Pick the tint on purpose. Cool blue-greys give a crisp, clean white; brown or sepia tones give a natural or aged white. A flat grey mixed from black and white looks dull.
Thin light layers either a lot and build several coats, or place a small thick dab and feather its edge with a damp brush. Normal layer thickness is where chalky streaks come from.

Over red or black, base in an off-white, which covers better than pure white, in three or so thin coats, letting each dry. Or paint a mid blue first, then two parts white to one of blue, and the white covers in a stroke or two. Red pigment hides in brushes and turns white pink, so rinse well first.
White dries a little darker than it looks wet, so judge each coat dry. If white paint goes on chalky, white ink is opaque but smooth for tidy-ups and small points.

Save pure white for a few edges and shiny points; many painters stop at a pale bone or blue-grey. Add dark lining where a hard shadow would fall, but between two white parts, such as gloved fingers, use a mid blue rather than black, which looks too stark.

guides.title: Painting yellow
guides.summary: Shade yellow with warm oranges and browns, never black or grey, and give it a pale or warm undercoat.
body: Yellow is see-through. Over black or dark grey it turns greenish and dull. Prime white, bone, pink or yellow, sprayed in short light bursts so detail does not clog. Yellow shows every mould line and bubble, and its pigment settles, so clean up well and shake or stir the paint each time.
Over pink with white dusted from above, a yellow one-coat paint turns orange in the recesses and shades itself. Peach gives a softer, browner shade.

Over black, block the yellow areas in first with a light grey, a thinned off-white or a deep, high-coverage yellow in two or three smooth coats, then paint the bright yellow over it. Any texture underneath shows through.

If it still needs many coats, add one each time you pause on another area so it is dry when you return. A dense, slightly ochre yellow covers far faster, and also looks more like dyed cloth than a fluorescent pure yellow. Parts that come off, such as a helmet, are quicker primed white on their own.

Shading yellow with black or grey makes it look green and dirty. Shade with a deeper golden or ochre yellow, then a sepia or warm brown run into the recesses, and a mid brown only in the deepest gaps. Let a wash pool and leave it alone to dry; moving it or blasting it with a hair dryer turns it muddy.
If yellow already looks lime in the shadows, glaze a thin reddish orange over the lower areas. Red cancels green. Test the strength on a small area first.

For highlights, a cream or bone looks soft and natural, while a paler yellow looks crisp and stark. If pale yellow over a pale undercoat ends with no contrast, put shadow back with a thin dark brown and bring yellow back on the raised parts.
On yellow and black models, finish the yellow first and paint the black up to it. Black covers slips on yellow easily; yellow does not cover black, and mistakes on yellow are slow to fix.

guides.title: Painting pale skin
guides.summary: Build pale skin from pinks and very pale tones, with cool highlights and warm shadows, and avoid browns.
body: Browns add a tan. Build pale skin from pinks and very pale flesh tones instead, adding a little more pink with each layer. A ready-made flesh cooled with a light blue also reads paler.
Give highlights and shadows opposite temperatures: push a little cool blue into the highlights and keep the shadows warm.
Lay out about five paints from dark to light and mix half steps between them for around ten tones. Use the very lightest and darkest mostly for mixing.

Over black primer, a thin mid grey under the skin lets pale tones cover in one coat and cools them slightly. An undercoat of pale cold blue from above and red from below maps the light before you start.

Skin made only from pinks looks flat, and pale skin built from yellowish or greenish tones looks sickly. Glaze a thin magenta into cheeks, lips and joints, and a muted grey-blue into the shadows and where skin looks thinner.
Keep these glazes very thin and build them slowly so they tint rather than cover. If warm shading spreads too far, the skin reads pink or purple instead of pale.
Chalky pale skin comes from light layers that never fully cover the darker ones. Step up slowly and give each layer two or three thin coats; shading down from a light base is often easier.
For cold, wintry skin, highlight with a cold off-white and glaze a thin red onto the cheeks, nose and ears. For a pallid, unwell look, glaze thin magenta and violet into the shadows instead.

guides.title: Making plain sculpts interesting
guides.summary: Grime, war paint, eyebrows and skin colour shifts add story to bland or overly clean sculpts.
body: If a model looks too clean for what it is meant to be, the fix is usually in the paint, not the sculpt.
Shift the skin. Cool and desaturate it, and slip in hints of pink, purple or sickly green for a feral or undead look.
Add mud splatter on feet, legs and cloth hems, where the figure would really get dirty.
Freehand simple war paint or tattoo shapes on bare skin. Make the leader's the most elaborate.
Paint eyebrows. They give a face expression and stop it looking flat.
Keep what already works, such as clean armour, and only change the parts that help the story.

guides.title: Pushing contrast further
guides.summary: Small models need darker shadows and brighter highlights than seem natural, so push both further than feels right.
body: Tiny sculpted features cannot cast real shadows, so you have to paint the light and dark in, as an illustrator would on a flat picture.
The smaller the model or detail, the more you exaggerate. Very large models need less. Small belts and symbols need a thin, clean dark line around them; thick black lines look crude.

When you think highlights and shadows are right, push the highlights brighter and the shadows deeper again, two or three times. If you overshoot, glaze the thinned base colour over the whole surface to pull it back.

Highlights look brighter next to darker shadows. Deepen the down-facing areas with the base mixed with a deep blue, purple or black before pushing the highlights further. Use deep shades and light tints of the colour itself, not only black and white, and take shadow mixes from colours already on the palette.

To reset your eye, paint one cheap model with shadows taken right down to black and highlights right up to white. It looks overdone up close but grabs attention from across a room. Then paint one your usual way; your normal level of contrast usually moves up. Your own sense of normal drifts, so compare with strong work side by side.
Edge highlights and dark lining in recesses are simple ways to add value contrast. Where two shapes should separate, put a dark line with a light line either side.
Rather than adding many small steps near the top, a bold jump to a stark final highlight on the sharpest points often reads better. Put the brightest highlights around the face to pull the eye there.

Do not lose contrast chasing smoothness. Judge the model at arm's length under normal room light, which flattens subtle work. If you will weather it, overdo the contrast first, as filters, washes and dust knock it back.

guides.title: Researching historical uniform colours
guides.summary: Use period photos, surviving garments and books to get uniform colours right, and allow for real variation.
body: Before painting a historical figure, gather pictures of the real uniform and kit from the period and place. Photos of surviving garments, or a museum visit, are more reliable than painted illustrations, which often drift in colour.

Military history books and online collections show the right colours, insignia and camouflage patterns. Read a little about the unit and the conditions it served in, such as desert, winter or a long campaign.

There is no single exact colour. Real cloth varied between dye batches, faded in the sun and wore with use, so pick whatever paint looks right to you for a named colour, such as a greenish grey for a grey field uniform.

Many later uniforms sit in greens, olives and browns. Paint camouflage as broken shapes over the base colour rather than tidy outlines, and keep it a little softer than the reference so it reads at scale.
Small models look darker than the real thing, so lighten the reference colour a touch. Finish with chalk pastels or dry pigments for dust and earth where the figure meets the ground.

guides.title: Shading without black
guides.summary: Shade with deep hues, the opposite colour or the scheme's middle colour instead of black, which dulls colours.
body: Black, white and grey drain saturation from a colour. Shade with a rich dark colour instead, such as a deep blue, purple, deep red or dark green.

The simplest pick is a deeper neighbour on the colour wheel, one to three steps round: yellow shades with orange or red, blue with purple, yellow-green with turquoise or blue. Purple also sits well under warm orange and beige, and dark brown under pale sand and stone.

The opposite colour works in small amounts. A touch of red darkens a bright green, and a thin dark green glaze deepens a red, without going grey. Too much of either turns the mix brown, which only helps if you want a dirty look.
Some colours are naturally darker. Pure blue, red and purple are much darker than yellow and green, so you can shade with hue as well as value.
In a narrow scheme, the colour that sits in the middle of your range often makes the best shadow. In a blue and turquoise scheme with a hint of magenta, that is a purple.
Highlight with a lighter colour of similar hue, a pale yellow or a bone rather than plain white. On skin, a dark red shadow and a pale yellow or pale orange highlight keep it warm and alive.
A shade does not have to be darker. A see-through yellow over drybrushed pink pools into warm orange-brown shadows, and a pink wash in the recesses of grey-purple skin adds colour without dirt.

Black is fine for the very deepest gaps, or for a deliberately grim, ashy look. For a smoky, worn look, mix each colour's shadow with a shared brown instead, which also ties a group together. Big patches of pure black, for example on a base, read as holes rather than shadow.

guides.title: Colours for terrain and scenery
guides.summary: Keep scenery dull so models stand out, with one restrained accent colour.
body: Use greys, dull metals and browns for most of the piece. Scenery is a backdrop, not the subject, and it sits beside a board and other pieces. Warm light greys suit most boards and do not fight with bright models.

Add one muted accent that suits the setting, such as a mustard yellow, a faded red, cool green moss for a temperate board or orange rust for a hot one. A single masked stripe across a big plain wall, or a few pipes picked out in copper, breaks up large areas in minutes.

Prime black into every recess, then dust dark grey lightly from above to show the detail. If you airbrush higher, stop at a cool grey; the later weathering is warm and brown, and a cool start balances it.
Base coat roughly with a large old brush. Speed matters more than neatness, slight patchiness reads as age, and drybrushing does most of the work. Skip picking out every rivet.
Stir a pinch of sand into paint for gritty flat surfaces.
Paint every building in a set the same way, and note the primer, marking colour and wash colours you used, so new pieces match the old ones later.
For a display or diorama, repeat the patterns and palette from the figures on walls, flags and props so models and scenery read as one piece.
A brighter classic look also works: a few strong colours over neutral stone, light grime and crisp edge highlights. Choose one look for the whole table.

guides.title: Testing a scheme before painting
guides.summary: Try colours as stripes, on a spare part or as a digital mock-up before committing to the model.
body: Paint small stripes or a quick grid of swatches: each base colour with a few mixed steps from dark to light beside it. Hold a grey value scale next to them to check there is enough light and dark. If two steps look too similar or too far apart, change one now. Keep the card beside you while you paint.
Test over the same colour as your undercoat. The same paints look very different over black and over white.
Put a little of each paint on paper both pure and thinned with water. Thinning reveals hidden tints; a deep red may turn out quite purple.

Paint a spare part, an old model or a cheap figure with the full scheme first. Many kits include a spare head that makes a small test bust on a cork, and different trim options on one spare model are easy to compare side by side.

For a digital mock-up, photograph the primed model and colour over it with a soft, low-opacity brush in any free drawing program, or use colour blend layers in an image editor. No art skill is needed, and ten schemes take half an hour.

Without a computer, print a photo of the primed model and paint on it with the real paints, or colour a greyscale print or line drawing with pencils. Some apps let you paint a 3D model, but metallics and bases rarely look right there.
For an army, paint one test model and time each step, then adjust the plan over the next two or three.
If the test looks dark and muddy, start again from a brighter, more saturated base and keep the coloured steps over larger areas before the pale highlight.

guides.title: Tinting whites, greys and blacks
guides.summary: Lean whites, greys and blacks towards a hue so they feel warm, cold or tied to the rest of the scheme.
body: Plain neutral white, grey and black can look flat. Lean them slightly towards a colour instead, ideally one used elsewhere on the model.
A little brown in the greys gives a natural, warm white such as fur or old cloth.
A little blue gives a cold white. A warm green feels organic.
A bright blue can even serve as the shade colour for a white area, with a pale blue-grey or green as its highlight.
Reuse the highlight colour of the main armour or cloth on neutral parts so everything looks lit by the same light.
Keep the tinted base mix on the palette and add white to it for each lighter step, so every step shares the tint.
If a finished white looks too stark, thin a sepia or light brown wash into a filter and brush it over the whole area to turn it into a softer off-white.
On grey skin, base in a warm red-tinted grey and step up towards a cool green-tinted grey. A very thin pinkish filter on the cheeks, muzzle and inner joints makes it read as living, not stone.

guides.title: Two-tone cloaks
guides.summary: Paint a cloak's lining a different, usually darker, colour from the outside so the figure stands out from it.
body: Choose a brighter tone for the outer face of the cloak and a deeper one for the lining and under layers.
The darker lining frames the body and keeps parts from blending into each other.
The lining can also be a contrasting colour, such as red inside a dark green cloak, for a more striking look.
A weak see-through paint mixed with a darker, stronger one gives better coverage and a richer lining colour.
A warm red-brown leather on belts and boots stands out well against a lot of green.

guides.title: Kinds of contrast
guides.summary: Contrast is any difference, in light and dark, hue, temperature, saturation, shape or texture, and each helps a model read.
body: Value contrast, light next to dark, matters most. A bright line beside a dark one makes detail jump out. When someone says an area needs more contrast, make the highlights brighter, the shadows darker, or both.

Hue contrast pairs colours from opposite sides of the colour wheel, such as red with green or orange with teal. It works best when one of the pair clearly dominates, and a small touch hidden in shadows, like turquoise in the recesses of copper, adds it quietly.
Warm next to cool makes the warm look warmer and the cool cooler.
Saturation contrast: one strong colour among greys or muted tones stands out strongly.
Shape, texture and finish contrast: soft faces against hard armour, rough dusty surfaces against clean shiny ones, matt black beside gloss black. The base can add contrast too.

Area matters. A large highlight with a tiny shadow looks less contrasted than the same colours with more dark. Small markings need contrast with what is under them: black on mid grey vanishes at table distance, a strong red reads.
Alternate light and dark parts: pale armour with dark trim, dark armour with bright trim. A highlight next to deep shadow looks brighter than it is, so you often do not need white.

Check by turning a photo black and white; each part should still separate. Then read the symptom: muddy or dull needs a bigger light and dark gap, garish needs the loudest colours toned down, flat needs a second colour and varied values, washed out needs some darks, and cluttered needs fewer colours.

guides.title: Dead, undead and sickly skin
guides.summary: Drain a normal skin tone with grey or cold colours, keep a hint of warmth low down, and stain it with rot colours.
body: Start from a normal flesh and drain it with grey, black or a pale grey-green, which cancels some of the red. Leaving the orange out entirely gives deathly pale skin; a little green gives a second, sicker variant. For a vampiric, bloodless look, keep the pinks out of cheeks and lips and set the skin against strong red and black.
Highlight with a pale grey, khaki or bone rather than pure white or a warm yellow, or go cold with a pale violet and then a pale blue for menace. Light grey alone can look artificial on grey skin.

Keep a little warmth in the wash or the deepest shadows. Green-only skin reads as dead but lifeless; a thin crimson or purple in recesses, knees, elbows and joints makes the cold highlights stand out.

For diseased skin, mix a green into the shadow and midtone mixes and a cold yellow into the highlights. Stipple and dab rather than laying smooth layers; rough texture on skin reads as unwell. For a group of sickly creatures, a desaturated sandy yellow over bone, washes and a few edge highlights is quick.
A grey with colour in it beats plain grey. Base in a dark plum, then layer up by mixing in more and more green, always keeping a little purple. Touch pure pale green only on the very highest points.
Before highlighting, run thin deep crimson around wounds and under the eyes so they look sore and bloodshot, and drop a deep red into every hole and pock mark as old blood.

For rot, stain natural shadows with a thin turquoise, then add a thin magenta more selectively once dry. To show stages of decay across several bodies, vary the highlight: pale yellow for fresh, pale khaki-green for rotting, pale icy blue for long dead.
Keep clothing in neutral greys so it does not fight the skin, and shade white cloth and grey hair with a soft blue rather than brown. Dot the eyes with a milky off-white and skip the pupils.

guides.title: Tying an army together with colour
guides.summary: Repeat a spot colour, a small shared set of paints and the same shadow tone so different models read as one force.
body: Choose one vivid spot colour that contrasts with the main scheme, such as a glowing blue on red, and put it on every model: lenses, lights, gems or buttons. When one unit has a different main colour, carry the army colour onto its small areas, such as a tabard, a lining or a wax seal, using the same paints and steps.
Use the same small set of paints across every unit, heroes and troops alike. The same red recipe wherever red appears does more for unity than any single detail.
Share the shadow tone. One shadow colour, such as a dark magenta, used in the recesses of every model, weapon and base acts like shared ambient light.

Share the top highlight too: mix one tint into the final highlight of every material. Highlighting old and new batches with the same colours also ties them together when their base colours differ slightly.

On leaders and big models, use exactly the troops' recipe for shared parts, then add one or two extra steps on top. Put colours on infantry in the same places they sit on the big models. A vehicle need not match the uniform exactly if it shares the primer, highlights and a few accents.
Keep markings and glow effects in colours you already use. Any extra colour should be muted with black or its opposite, or replaced with off-white or black.
To tell units apart, vary one element such as shield colour or a trim, and keep everything else the same. Or pick three scheme colours and use only two on each trooper, swapped around.
Base every model the same way, and note the colours you used so figures painted months later still match.

guides.title: Using value in a scheme
guides.summary: Light and dark value is the backbone of a scheme; one colour at several values reads as one scheme without repeating.
body: Value is how light or dark a colour is. It does more to make a model read than the choice of hue: a model painted only in greys still shows light, shadow and material.
Use one scheme colour at different values on different areas: dark on the cloak, mid on the armour, light on the trim.

Make neighbouring areas differ in value, not just in hue, or they merge from a distance. Put light next to mid and dark next to either, never dark against dark. Dark leather or fur beside bright cloth frames it, and dark weathered metal can supply a missing dark.
If every colour sits in the middle of the range, nothing stands out. Let the most important areas, usually the face, reach the brightest values, and keep less important areas lower down darker.

The midtones decide what colour an area reads as. Keep most of the surface close to the target colour and use odd shading colours only in the transitions. To add variety, mix a different hue in at the same lightness, so it looks identical in a greyscale photo. The final bright highlight only needs about a fifth of the area.

To vary a colour, make it lighter, darker, brighter or duller before reaching for a new hue. Lighten with white or a white ink so the hue does not drift, though purple goes chalky unless a warm magenta goes in first. Darken with black or a deep colour of the same family. To dull a colour without changing its value, add a little of its opposite.

Each area only uses part of the range. In a lit area the darkest tone is around the middle of the scale; in a shadowed area the brightest tone is. You need the full contrast across the whole model, not on every plate.
Check values with a black and white photo. If two areas look the same grey, change one.

guides.title: Varying skin tones in a group
guides.summary: Shift skin tone figure to figure so a squad does not look like clones, while keeping one shared thread.
body: Identical skin across a small group makes the figures look like clones.
Give each one a slightly different tone: one warmer, one cooler, one paler, one darker.
A quick way on a batch: run the final all-over wash across the skin on some models and keep it off the skin on others, or give a few a grey or paler tone.
Keep a common thread so they still read as one group, such as the same shade colour, the same desaturated hue or the same final highlight.
Matching clothing, weapons and bases hold the group together even when the skin varies a lot.
Vary small details too, such as hair colour, war paint patterns, or a touch of red under the eyes and around scars.

guides.title: Telling browns and leathers apart
guides.summary: Separate leathers, straps and pouches by value and warmth, often by tinting one brown, so they do not merge.
body: A model covered in leather turns into one dull brown mass if every strap, pouch and boot is a similar brown.
You need few paints. Take one mid brown and mix in a little white, yellow, red, green, black or ivory for each item. Each mix still reads as leather, and the shared base keeps them in harmony.
Separate by value first. Place light next to dark and never put two dark or two pale leathers side by side. One very dark brown, one mid warm brown and one bright orange brown is a simple set.
Separate by warmth too. Start one leather from a red brown and another from a greenish olive brown, then highlight one with a yellowish tone and the other with a neutral pale tan.

Pouches and belts are often canvas or webbing, so they need not be brown. Black looks tidy against red armour, and olive green sits opposite red for stronger contrast. A brown canvas bag can still sit apart from straps: base it chocolate, edge it with a lighter beige brown, and keep the straps a darker oxide brown.
Run one dark brown wash only into the recesses and the joins between parts. The shared shadow ties the pieces together and still separates each one.
Skin can stay in the brown family if you push it more orange. Break up a large area of fur with a simple pattern, such as darker diamonds.
If a brown is not working, change direction rather than stacking more coats. A red brown shade can rescue a pale leather that looks flat.

guides.title: Varying colours across a unit
guides.summary: Spread a short list of cloth, uniform or horse colours across a unit so it looks natural but still belongs together.
body: Pick a short list of four or five colours you like and find easy, such as two light tans, a dark brown and a greenish khaki. Use them on jackets, trousers and gear, combined differently on each figure.

On repeated sculpts, keep the same set of colours but move them around: one figure with a black hood and grey shirt, the next with a red hood and dark trousers. The shared palette keeps the group unified.

For a uniformed unit, keep one shade colour, such as a dark brown, on every coat and vary only the highlight colour or how far you take it. Real issued cloth faded and came from different makers, so a few greener or greyer coats look right. Keep an older uniform to about one figure in five.

For troops without uniforms, mix freely: hose with each leg a different colour, a stripe down one side, a garment split into two colours or a contrasting trim. Do not repeat the same pattern on neighbouring figures, and vary metal too, with some helmets iron and some bronze.

For horses, group coat colours into light, mid and dark, such as white, grey and black or chestnut, light bay and dark bay. In a unit of six, paint three in your easiest colour, two in a second and one in a third, mixing light and dark.

Aim between the extremes. Every figure or horse a different colour distracts from the group; every one the same looks flat. Keep most harness or kit one colour and change it on one or two, and change the mix from unit to unit so they do not look identical.

guides.title: Balancing warm and cool across a model
guides.summary: Give a warm main colour cool details and a cool one warm details, including on the base, so parts stand apart.
body: If the main colour is warm, such as orange skin, give minor details like straps and leather cooler tones by adding a touch of blue to their mixes. A model full of rust, brass and brown blurs together until it gets a small blue-green prop, algae or verdigris.

If the main colours are cool, a warm copper, brass, reddish brown leather or a burgundy mouth makes both stand out and stops small details disappearing. On a warm model, black hair highlighted with a light blue sets off the reds beside it.
Keep the accent and the secondary colours smaller and less bright than the main one so they sit back. Knock a loud warm metal back with washes if it dominates.
Temperature also works through neighbours. A little blue or turquoise in a black wash run beside gold or yellow makes the gold look warmer and crisper without repainting it.
Carry a little of the main colour into the contrasting area, such as green verdigris on copper beside green armour, so the model still feels tied together.
On bases, set cool grey rocks on warm sandy ground, or warm stone on cool grey ground. Wash rocks darker before highlighting so they read as a separate material.
For repeated details such as parchment or seals, mix warm and cool versions so they do not all look identical.

Warm colours seem to come forward and cool ones sit back, and a mostly warm scheme feels lively or harsh, a cool one calm or eerie. Changing temperature between skin, armour and bone also tells the eye the material has changed.

guides.title: Warm and cool shadows and highlights
guides.summary: Give shadows and highlights opposite temperatures within one area for extra contrast without extra brightness.
body: Light and shadow differ in temperature as well as brightness. Making one warm and the other cool adds contrast.

Decide where the light comes from first. Keep the warm tones on the parts facing the light and the cool tones only in the deepest shadows on the far side. Deep shadows added evenly on both sides look blobby.
Warm shadow, cool highlight: wash a dark brown or a thin warm flesh-red into the recesses of grey-blue or blue armour, then highlight with lighter grey-blue and an off-white for a cold, pale finish.
On cool green armour, run warm browns into panel lines, pits and rivets. It ties the armour to warm skin and adds a grimy feel.

Cool shadow, warm highlight: shade blue with a purple, then use a pale yellow-green rather than white for the brightest spots. On red armour or red skin, glaze blue, purple or a muted green into the shadows and keep the highlights towards orange. On green skin, warm yellow glazes on muscle tops and cool blue below.

A simple pair for sunny, outdoor models is a warm pale skin-like tone as the highlight and a deep violet as the shadow; it suits nearly any colour. For snowy, cold scenes, flip it: cold bluish highlights over a deep crimson shadow.

A muted blue sketched onto the shadow sides of panels suggests cool bounced light and adds volume to a single-colour model. Steel can be warmed with a touch of brown in its black shade so it contrasts with cold armour.

Mixing a little of the main colour into the shadow colour helps the whole scheme hold together. Temperature also shapes volume: a cool glaze plays down a bump and a warm one softens a hollow, since warm seems to come forward and cool to sink back.

guides.title: Warm flush on skin
guides.summary: Thin warm reds on cheeks, knuckles, joints and ears make painted skin look alive, and a warm glaze rescues dull skin.
body: Thin a mid red, or a red mixed with some of the skin colour, until it is soft and see-through. For a faint filter, go to about six parts water or medium to one of paint; one coat should barely show.

Touch it onto knuckles, knees, elbows, ears, lips, scars and the sides of the cheeks, and into deep creases such as between fingers, where blood sits near the surface. A little around the eyes makes a figure look tired; on the nose and cheeks it looks ruddy and cheerful.
Work one area at a time and feather the edge outwards with a damp brush while it is wet, so there is no hard line.

On green, olive or yellow skin, a pink flesh colour on the joints often looks better than pure red. On cold pale skin, a violet-red filter around the eyes, lips and creases makes the cold look colder.

If skin has gone grey and dead, glaze a warm orange flesh mix (#d9792e with some skin tone) thinly over the whole area, and a thin bright red (#c42a24) on the sides of the head and in deep recesses. On skin meant to stay grey, a thin reddish glaze in the recesses and round eyes, mouth and knuckles makes it read as living flesh, not stone.

If flesh is simply too pale, several very thin red glazes into the shadows pink it up without repainting. A very thin orange over the transitions between highlight and shadow reads as warmth rather than orange.
A faint pale yellow glaze from the edge of the highlights down into the midtones warms skin like sunlight and hides rough transitions. Build it in two or so barely visible coats.
Keep it subtle; strong flushes look cartoonish. Do not push top highlights too white either, or the face will glare when seen from above.

guides.title: Wash or one-coat paint
guides.summary: A wash shades colours you have already painted; a contrast-style one-coat paint colours and shades in one step.
body: A wash goes over existing colours. It mostly sits in recesses, only lightly tints raised areas and keeps metallics shiny. Use it to shade and keep your colours.

A contrast-style one-coat paint does the base colour and shading together. It pools in recesses, leaves a thin tint on raised areas and dries matt. Over white, light grey or a zenithal prime it looks bright and clean; over dark primer it looks muted. Results are consistent model to model, which suits batch painting.
Test on the palette: spread a wash thin and it goes pale; a one-coat paint stays strong.
Over finished base coats, a one-coat paint can darken everything a lot. A bright red can end up near black.
One-coat paints that settle into a pale layer in the pot cover more like paint. Ones that do not behave more like inks and let metallics shine through.

Thinned with its clear medium, a one-coat paint dries slower than a wash, so it shades smoothly without tide marks and pulls less hard into recesses. You can steer it into the lower half of rounded shapes.
One-coat paints suit gaming pieces, especially organic models, but their built-in highlights are weak. Add an opaque edge highlight afterwards.
Colours in the same range behave differently, and thin glazes of them can look patchy. Test each on a spare piece.

guides.title: Washes and tints on metallics
guides.summary: Each wash colour changes a metal's character, but too much wash or a one-coat paint dulls the shine.
body: Every layer over a metallic hides some of the flakes that make it shine. For bright metal, keep washes to recesses, rivets and edges, or wash all over on purpose and then layer the metal back on raised areas with a brighter dot on the high points.

Over silver: blue gives cold steel, black gives dark iron, brown or yellow gives oily or aged metal, and sepia warms it towards gold. A black wash mixed half and half with a coloured wash gives a tinted steel.

Over gold: purple looks rich, green looks aged or tarnished, red or yellow deepen the warmth. A red wash pushes copper warmer. After a green tint on gold, edge with silver, as a paler gold gives too little contrast.

A wash stays see-through and keeps most of the shine. A one-coat paint tints strongly but goes matt, so thin it heavily and drybrush the metal back on edges. Matt washes dull metal and gloss ones look wet and run; a half and half mix dries satin.

A thin blue or turquoise glaze on the lower, down-facing parts of steel breaks up flat grey. Use ink, heavily diluted, with little on the brush, and keep the top highlights less blue so it still reads as steel. Glaze thin silver back over if it goes too far.

Very thin brown on down-facing surfaces and blue on up-facing ones gives a ground and sky effect. Tinting steel with a colour already in the scheme ties it in, and a different tint separates two metals on one model.
Washing dark acrylic all over metal can leave tide marks and kill the polish. For clean metal, shade with an oil wash or ink in the recesses.

Check what your black wash leans towards, warm or cool, and test mixes on a painted spot first. Spray and pot versions of one metallic often differ in warmth, so touch-ups may not match. For an army, paint all metal one way and vary only the wash per part: brown for age, black for grime, red brown for rust.

guides.title: Tough, weathered skin
guides.summary: A yellow-brown mid tone makes skin look thick, rough and older, while pink reads soft and young.
body: Pick three paints far apart in value, such as a dark red, a yellow-brown and a peach, and mix steps between them.
Coat all the skin in the dark red, then layer up with more yellow-brown, then peach. Leave the ears, eye sockets and sides of the nose darker as you go.
Glaze back over harsh layer lines as you go.
Work broad first. Pick out fine detail only in the top highlights: nose, knuckles, scars and folds.

For old, thin skin, build the pale tones in loose dabs and let the warm base show through in spots. Alternate very thin passes with a few thicker dabs of light; if too much goes on, dab it with a dry fingertip.
Follow the sculpted wrinkles: touch the crests, leave the folds dark, and add short pale lines where they catch light, with dots on the cheekbones.

Upward-facing planes should not drop darker than the mid tone, and hidden areas should top out at the mid tone. Bald heads easily end up too bright, so keep the palest tones mostly on the forehead and nose.
A touch of purple in a dark tone under the eyes and in the cheek hollows, and pink in the lower lip, add life. For a softer, younger look, lean the mid tone towards pink instead of yellow-brown.

guides.title: Where highlights go
guides.summary: Highlight the tops of shapes and anything that sticks out, brighter higher up, from one chosen light direction.
body: With ordinary light from above, highlight upward-facing surfaces and parts that protrude towards the viewer. Look straight down on the model: whatever you can see gets the first highlight, and each lighter layer is the same shape, smaller.

Treat each part separately: helmet, each armour plate, sleeve, trouser leg. Push the highlight to the top of each, where it meets the fold or material above. Highlighting the middle or bottom of a part is the usual mistake.

A surface is brightest where it faces the light head-on and darkens as it turns away. Picture arms as cylinders and heads as spheres to see how that falls; a bald head or helmet gets its bright spot on the side facing the light.

Pick a light direction, usually above and slightly to one side, and leave the side facing away in the darker tone. Edge the shadow side with a duller tone and the lit side with a brighter one. Sharp folds get a hard dark line, gentle slopes a soft fade.

Light weakens lower down. Mix two or three values of the highlight: the brightest on the top tenth near the face, a slightly darker one on the top half, and duller ones lower down. A face may take three or four highlight stages while boots get one or none. Spend more steps on centrepiece models.
Bounced light from the ground does the opposite and gets a little stronger and cooler low down, so hidden undersides should not be pure black.

While shading, keep the centres of raised panels clean; those patches show where highlights go. A zenithal spray of white from above over dark primer maps the light on matt surfaces. Or hold the primed model under a single lamp or torch, turn it slowly, and highlight only where the glare lands.

Watch for shapes that break the pattern, such as a form bulging near its bottom. For a glow from below, reverse the rules. Edging every edge equally is a stylised alternative that reads crisply at arm's length but does not match one light, and small vehicles often read better lit as if from several sides.

guides.title: Colour gradients across a whole model
guides.summary: Shift a colour plate by plate across the model, such as red at the feet to yellow at the head.
body: Instead of one colour all over, shift the colour across the model, for example deep red at the boots, orange in the middle and orange-yellow on the shoulders and helmet.
Give each armour plate its own flat colour. Because each plate is distinct, no wet blending is needed; the steps from plate to plate make the gradient.
Mix the in-between colours from their neighbours, such as red with orange, so each step looks related rather than like a new colour.
Put the brightest, warmest colour at the head and shoulders. It draws the eye to the face.
Bright yellows at the top end cover poorly. A strongly pigmented paint, or a white or pale undercoat on those plates, saves a lot of coats.

For highlights, one shared highlight colour across the whole gradient ties it together. Or highlight each zone with its own colour mixed with a light grey, adding a second, lighter step on the outward edges. Both work; pick one and keep to it.

guides.title: Why metallics can look flat
guides.summary: Real metallic paint reflects real light at miniature scale, so on small models it can look like a toy.
body: A miniature stands for something much larger, but real light falls on it as if it were tiny.
That is why we paint shading at all. A base coat under a desk lamp never looks like a big object.
Metallic paint relies on real light, so on a small model its shine can look small and toy-like.
Fix it by shading and highlighting the metal strongly: dark recesses and bright edges and dots.
Painted reflections with matt paint let you exaggerate contrast further. Metallic paint suits larger pieces, such as busts and statues, especially well.

To compare metallics, paint each on the same simple shape or a strip of black card and turn it slowly under a lamp. Watch the dark reflections as well as the bright ones; that contrast is what sells metal.
A metallic that stays evenly bright from every angle covers well but reads flat, more like grey paint than steel. It can still make a useful base coat under a brighter metallic.
